content.title: The generalist — healthcare’s multi-tool
content.description: For healthcare to become sustainable, primary care must be built on generalists and a holistic approach, rather than the silo logic of hospitals. How can governance and organisation reverse the trend towards ever greater specialisation?
content.extendedDescription: The seminar takes the opinion article “Primärvården är inte ett sjukhus i miniatyr” as its starting point and highlights the generalist’s central role in a sustainable healthcare system. It explores how primary care built on breadth, continuity and a holistic perspective delivers better care, lower costs and a robust organisation. The panel examines why today’s governance drives subspecialisation, how this affects patients and staff, and what is needed to reverse the trend. By bringing together healthcare professionals, regional leadership and national politicians, the seminar creates a constructive, practical discussion about the decisions and organisational changes needed to strengthen generalist expertise and make the transition to close-to-home care succeed.

content.title: Should your postcode determine whether you have a regular doctor?
content.description: Where you live in Sweden, within a region, or even your street address determines your chance of having a regular doctor. What can be done to make a regular doctor a reality for everyone in the country?
content.extendedDescription: Access to a regular doctor in primary care is at rock bottom when Sweden is compared with similar countries. There are several reasons for this, but the decision to transition to Nära vård has clearly established that primary care should be both the foundation and the hub of healthcare. To make this possible, primary care needs to be expanded, particularly access to specialists in general practice. In 2022, Socialstyrelsen set the benchmark for the number of residents a regular primary care doctor can look after at 1100. Reaching this target requires roughly doubling the number of specialists in general practice in the country, but they must also be distributed reasonably evenly so that all residents receive equitable care. A few regions are already within reach of the benchmark, while several others face a long, steep uphill climb. How do we ensure that everyone has access to a knowledgeable, available specialist in general practice?

content.title: The right to vote — are elections accessible to people with extensive disabilities?
content.description: Does everyone really have the same opportunity to exercise their right to vote? People with extensive disabilities face barriers when voting: lack of awareness of the right to take a personal assistant behind the voting screen, inadequate physical accessibility and treatment that is not adapted to individual needs.
content.extendedDescription:
The right to vote is fundamental in a democracy, but for people with extensive disabilities, major communication difficulties or reduced intellectual ability, elections are far from always accessible in practice.

The most common problem is that election workers refuse to let voters take their personal assistant behind the screen, even though this is their right. The same problem can arise with mobile voting. Staff’s lack of knowledge risks depriving people of their democratic right.

Physical accessibility is also crucial. This includes, for example, an effective right to priority for those who cannot stand in a queue, but also how people are treated: addressing the person concerned rather than the assistant or representative, and having the patience to wait for an answer.
We discuss what needs to change to make elections accessible to everyone, and who is responsible for making that happen.

content.title: Does every child have the right to grow up in a family?
content.description: In Sweden, children with disabilities can be placed in institutions instead of growing up in their family. This contravenes both the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Society must provide support that enables every child to live as part of their family.
content.extendedDescription:
Growing up in a family is a fundamental right — but for children with extensive disabilities, it is far from guaranteed. Special housing under LSS remains an option for children, which means that society can in practice place children in institutions when support at home is insufficient, for example when personal assistance is denied. Children without intellectual disabilities, on the other hand, can be placed with foster families. This is deeply discriminatory on the basis of IQ.

At the same time, there is a profound lack of knowledge about living conditions in families where someone has a disability. A common myth is that relatives work as personal assistants for convenience. The reality is often the opposite: family members who provide assistance contribute invaluable continuity, quality and security to the child’s everyday life.

The seminar takes the form of a conversation about what is required for all children in Sweden to have the right to grow up at home, society’s obligations, and how attitudes towards relatives as assistants need to change.
speakerTitles: Member of the Parliamentary Committee on Health and Welfare

content.title: Digital accessibility — when will Sweden have electronic identification for every citizen?
content.description: Many people with intellectual disabilities are denied BankID and thereby excluded from digital public services such as 1177, pharmacies and public authorities. A decision has been made on a register of legal representatives, but state electronic identification that works for every citizen is still awaited.
content.extendedDescription:
We are all citizens of equal human worth — but in digitalised Sweden, people with intellectual disabilities are treated worse than others. Without BankID, we are shut out of an increasing number of services that other citizens take for granted: healthcare advice, pharmacies, online shopping and public services. This discrimination on the basis of IQ must stop.

The technology for a solution exists. The register of legal representatives is part of new legislation. What is needed now is political will and ambition from public authorities to actually implement the plan for state electronic identification for everyone. Systems aimed at the public must also be accessible to people who have a legal representative (god man), with traceability and legal safeguards, but without special rules.

When will Sweden take responsibility for giving every citizen effective digital accessibility, and what is needed to get there?

content.title: Does every citizen have the right to equitable healthcare?
content.description: Those of us with intellectual and extensive disabilities can testify to being denied care, not being listened to and encountering prejudices that our lives are not worth living. This is a systemic failure. Everyone should have an equal right to care and a good life, regardless of intellectual ability.
content.extendedDescription:
Being denied emergency care. Having teeth extracted because the dentist thought you did not need them. A doctor talking over your head, as if you were not in the room. This is the reality for many people with intellectual disabilities and major communication difficulties when dealing with Swedish healthcare.

Prejudices about quality of life and human worth have no place in healthcare. Yet they influence which care is provided — and which is denied. The government has tasked Myndigheten för vård- och omsorgsanalys with mapping accessibility and the treatment of people with disabilities in healthcare.

In the conversation, we discuss what the mapping shows, what must change, and the responsibility of politicians and public authorities for ending discrimination on the basis of IQ.

content.title: Should welfare crime in personal assistance be investigated at the expense of assistance users’ freedom?
content.description: Welfare crime in personal assistance must be combated — but not at the cost of assistance users’ right to choose relatives both as legal representatives and as assistants when this is crucial for self-determination, communication and security.
content.extendedDescription:
The inquiry into more effective measures against welfare crime and greater predictability in personal assistance (Dir. 2025:40) focuses on relatives and how, by holding dual roles, they pursue their own interests and commit assistance allowance fraud.

In this seminar, we want to highlight that regulating relatives’ right to provide assistance risks restricting freedom of choice and the quality of assistance rather than curbing crime. Our reports “Anhöriga som ställföreträdare och personliga assistenter” and “Obefogad oro” highlight the lack of facts, but the abundance of attitudes and prejudices, surrounding claims that relatives with dual roles exploit or neglect their duties. Relatives who work as assistants often secure assistance by filling gaps in the rota and usually have the longest experience and greatest knowledge.

If assistance provided by relatives is curtailed, how will self-determination and the opportunity to live a free life with assistance be secured?

content.title: The assistance allowance is insufficient — what happens when safe, high-quality assistance cannot be provided?
content.description: The assistance allowance has been eroded for over a decade. For someone who depends on personal assistance, this is not a budget issue; it is a matter of life or death. When the allowance is insufficient, people risk being directed to institutions or group homes against their will.
content.extendedDescription:
Personal assistance is not a luxury. For many, it is the difference between surviving in their own home and losing their life in an institution. Many JAG members have experience of group homes, and several have testified that it nearly cost them their lives. The assistance allowance has been eroded for over ten years. The benchmark for collectively agreed wage increases is 3% for 2026. The allowance rose by 1.5%. The government promised indexation in the autumn budget. The promise was broken.

The allowance must cover reasonable wages, induction for new employees, supervision, continuing training, digital systems and more. It no longer does. The reform is slowly being strangled. Several reputable providers can manage another year — then they will be forced to close. When they disappear, the door opens to unscrupulous operators. Those who lose their assistance risk being forced to live with ageing parents or move into a group home — precisely what LSS was once intended to free them from.

Most importantly of all: it saves lives. Anyone could become one of us at any time.
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament, member of the Parliamentary Committee on Health and Welfare

content.title: Circular construction and clay in Sweden’s first NollCO₂ refurbishment
content.description: The construction industry accounts for a significant share of Sweden’s carbon dioxide emissions. Producing new building materials also burdens the environment in several ways. Reusing more materials and products can save both money and the environment. Our buildings make us ill; clay can help create a healthier indoor environment.
content.extendedDescription:
Kaminsky Arkitektur presents Signalhuset, an office building in Marievik, Stockholm, that is to be refurbished.
Signalhuset will be the first project in Sweden certified under SGBC’s NollCO₂ 2.0 for refurbishment. Reusing materials such as plasterboard, glass, marble floors and internal doors combines environmental care with architectural quality. The goal is Miljöbyggnad Guld and Energy Class A — an office as sustainable as it is beautiful.
After an introductory presentation, we invite a panel to discuss clay and circular construction in commercial properties. Where are we today? Where do we want to go?

content.title: Childhood trauma — the cost comes later
content.description: In Sweden, we tend to sweep difficult life crises and death out of sight. Grief can be seen as something strange that one ought to get over. But unprocessed grief and a complete lack of support for those affected can carry a high price in the future.
content.extendedDescription: Professor Mikael Rostila’s research has shown that major costs to society arise when we do not address and process grief. For children in particular, this can have serious consequences, including mental ill-health and other negative health effects. Today’s support for bereaved people is not designed to help those affected either. Healthcare struggles to make accurate diagnoses, and Försäkringskassan has rules that are not adapted to bereaved people’s needs. Better support can both help individuals and save society resources. How do politicians view these issues? Is it possible to change working methods in healthcare and other relevant bodies? What role can non-profit organisations play? Welcome to a panel discussion with experts and politicians organised by SAMS – Samarbete för Människor i Sorg.

content.title: How do we talk to children about death?
content.description: Children do not have the same perspective on death as adults. How do we talk to them about difficult life events and, in the worst case, death?
content.extendedDescription:
As an adult, it is difficult to put yourself in a child’s world. During extreme or traumatic life events such as the death of a relative, it is important to be present for the child rather than withdraw.
Researcher Rakel Eklund at Uppsala universitet specialises in children’s grief and how children experience difficult life events. She presents research findings that, when applied in practice, can make a major difference to families affected by grief and death. With the right support and understanding of children, we can create a more stable foundation for their future health and development.
The seminar takes the form of a presentation followed by an opportunity to ask questions about this difficult subject. It is hosted by SAMS – Samarbete för Människor i Sorg.

content.title: Everyone’s right to contribute at work — reality or utopia?
content.description:
In Sweden, people with extensive disabilities and a cognitive impairment are directed to separate activities in dedicated premises. Does it have to be this way?
Is it people who do not fit into working life — or working life that is not organised for everyone? What happens when we think differently?
content.extendedDescription:
The exhibition Stöd till Stordåd starts with a simple but crucial question:
What happens when we think differently about work and participation?
Through photographs and personal stories, the exhibition shows how people with extensive disabilities, supported by personal assistance, can be part of working life and contribute in ordinary workplaces.
It highlights experiences from workplaces where inclusion is a reality, not just an idea.
At the same time, the exhibition raises questions about the structures and assumptions that still limit access to working life, and about how it can be organised so that more people can participate, contribute and be part of the community.
The event is an open exhibition. The photographer is Magnus Selander.

content.title: Everyone’s right to contribute at work — from utopia to reality
content.description: In Sweden, people with extensive disabilities and a cognitive impairment are directed to separate activities in dedicated premises. Does it have to be this way? What happens when we think differently?
content.extendedDescription:
The exhibition Stöd till stordåd starts with the question: what happens when we think differently about work and participation?

Through photographs and personal stories, the exhibition shows how people with extensive disabilities, supported by personal assistance, can be part of working life and contribute in ordinary workplaces. It highlights workplaces where inclusion is a reality, not just an idea.

During the seminar, visitors hear directly from the participants about their experiences of work, community and participation. The exhibition also raises questions about the structures that still limit access to working life.

The event ends with an exhibition opening, where visitors can explore the exhibition and meet the participants behind the stories. The photographer is Magnus Selander.

content.title: When antibiotics stop working — how do we save tomorrow’s patients?
content.description:
Antibiotics are essential for surgical procedures and cancer treatments. Antibiotic resistance could make advanced surgery entirely impossible.
How can we prevent that situation?
content.extendedDescription:
Today, antibiotics are essential for all surgical procedures, cancer treatments and fighting severe infections. Around 25% of all inpatients in Swedish hospitals are receiving antibiotics, and antibiotics have revolutionised modern medicine. But antibiotic resistance is now increasing worldwide. This could potentially make advanced surgery entirely impossible. How can we prevent a situation in which we can no longer provide the healthcare we have become accustomed to?

To solve the problem, we need to tackle it from several directions. We must prevent infections from spreading, but also find new ways to treat and prevent sepsis, which is what makes infections life-threatening. Livestock farming currently accounts for most global antibiotic use, affecting the spread of resistance. To successfully combat antibiotic resistance, we must work on different solutions for people, animals and the environment throughout the world.
speakerTitles: Infectious diseases physician, Deputy State Epidemiologist

content.title: Models for defence research on campus — how do we protect security without stifling innovation?
content.description: As the tone of security policy grows increasingly strident and focuses on risks, academia has also been drawn in. How can higher education institutions conduct defence research while retaining creativity and taking a proportionate approach to security?
content.extendedDescription: As the tone of security policy grows increasingly strident and focuses on risks, academia has also been drawn in. Universities are developing increasingly strict rules for international cooperation while the EU is focusing more and more on expanding dual-use research. How can higher education institutions conduct defence research while retaining creativity and taking a proportionate approach to security? Are we becoming too caught up in security thinking and missing opportunities for better solutions that greater cooperation across borders and disciplines could enable? How are the cumulative effects of multiple regulatory frameworks handled? These questions become particularly acute in the growing number of civil-military collaborations at Swedish higher education institutions. In this discussion with representatives of Swedish universities and defence authorities, we examine the strengths and weaknesses of different collaboration models, drawing on a joint research security project involving FOI, Lunds universitet and Försvarshögskolan.

content.title: A new world order is emerging — how should the Nordic countries navigate it?
content.description: The global balance of power is changing dramatically. A new world order is emerging in which large, powerful countries claim the right to decide. Geopolitical tensions, hybrid threats and disinformation are creating uncertainty in Sweden and the Nordic region in ways we have not seen for decades. In a world where hostile state actors — and even allies — act unpredictably and against Nordic interests, the region must prepare for a new risk landscape.

The question is whether the Nordic countries are ready for these challenges. Is the Nordic region our salvation when cold winds blow around us, the place where we find security in troubled times?

This event explores what the new world order means for Nordic preparedness, democratic resilience and society’s ability to withstand threats and pressure.

content.title: A place of one’s own — towards housing policy that prevents violence
content.description: Access to permanent housing is crucial to enabling victims of violence to leave perpetrators and be protected from post-separation abuse. In Sweden, victims have no right to a new home when they need to leave because of violence, resulting in continuing insecurity, unstable housing and homelessness.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar addresses the importance of housing for the safety of women and children after leaving an abuser — an issue at the intersection of policy, research and practice.

NCK’s report En egen plats - våldsutsattas tillgång och rätt till trygga och stabila bostadsförhållanden is presented as a starting point for the discussion. The study examines how victims’ opportunities to obtain permanent housing are shaped by the interaction between legislation, municipal practice and housing policy. It shows how these structures affect the journey from violence and protection to recovery and freedom from violence, from the perspectives of professionals and victims and through analysis of regulations and their application.

The conversation highlights opportunities to strengthen victims’ access to permanent housing nationally and locally. How can housing have a greater role in work against gender-based violence, and how can violence become a priority in housing provision?

content.title: Older people with multiple conditions — healthcare’s greatest challenge?
content.description: Older people with multiple conditions face a high risk of unplanned hospital care. Neither national nor local reforms clearly reduce the need for hospital care — levels remain unchanged. How should healthcare be organised to achieve better long-term outcomes from coordinated health and social care?
content.extendedDescription: In most high-income countries, initiatives are under way to move care from hospitals into various forms of outpatient care. These initiatives differ according to how healthcare is governed and funded in each country. The goals are higher quality, greater person-centredness and more cost-effective healthcare. In international comparisons, Sweden often ranks relatively highly for concrete medical outcomes but frequently near the bottom for person-centredness, perceived continuity and coordination of healthcare. Since we all have “a system perfectly designed for the results we get”, we focus on the design and implementation of collaborative care. Is it empty talk, or could Sweden, with its unique position and collectively funded healthcare system, achieve substantially better results? Drawing on research, the conversation explores possible ways to achieve tangible outcomes.
speakerTitles: Programme leader for the National Dissemination Initiative, medical adviser, PhD

content.title: Digitalisation as a catalyst for sustainable construction —
content.description: Over the years, many reports and analyses have identified construction as one of the most conservative and least digitalised sectors. content.title: As a school staff member, may I physically restrain a pupil to protect other children?
content.description: School staff must maintain safety and a calm learning environment, but feel uncertain about their powers when a situation becomes urgent. How is children’s right to personal integrity balanced against staff’s duty to intervene — and what responsibility does the school authority have to provide clarity and legal certainty?
content.extendedDescription:
It is an ordinary school day. A conflict escalates. A chair is thrown. Pupils risk being injured. The teacher has seconds to act — or not. What are staff actually allowed to do? And what happens if they do nothing?

Since 2022, the Education Act has given school staff general powers to intervene to ensure safety and a calm learning environment. Despite this, many teachers and headteachers feel uncertain about boundaries, documentation and responsibility. Fear of complaints and criticism risks paralysing action in situations that require clear leadership.

The seminar starts from concrete, realistic scenarios and explores how the legislation should be interpreted in practice. We discuss how children’s right to personal integrity under the Convention on the Rights of the Child relates to schools’ duty to protect other pupils and staff, and the school authority’s responsibility to provide support, training and clear guidelines. The aim is to strengthen safety in schools through greater legal clarity, courage and legal certainty.

content.title: Who takes responsibility for Sweden’s circular transition when regulations do not?
content.description: Swedish regulations permit circularity, but do not require it. Although construction accounts for 40% of Sweden’s waste and a substantial climate impact, there are no mandatory policy instruments for reuse. The question is how regulations and requirements need to evolve to drive real change.

Upphandlingsmyndigheten offers voluntary circular criteria that public-sector clients can choose to disregard without consequences. Meanwhile, Boverket lacks the mandate to introduce binding requirements. The result is a construction sector that wants to make the transition, but where responsibility and governance remain inadequate. What is needed to move from voluntary action to clear rules for a circular economy?

content.title: Which political decisions are needed and promised to achieve sustainable construction during the next electoral term?
content.description: The election year marks the start of the term running until 2030 — a crucial period for meeting our climate targets. The property, construction and civil engineering industries believe we can still limit warming and meet the Paris Agreement, but clear political support through legislation, policy and financing is needed.
content.extendedDescription:
How can politics and construction together accelerate the transition? Join a dialogue with EU, national and municipal politicians about how the next electoral term can drive sustainable construction. The conversation focuses on responsibility, incentives and removing barriers to achieving the Paris Agreement’s goals.

content.title: A growing problem in Swedish schools: why is bullying allowed to continue?
content.description: Despite legal requirements and anti-bullying work, children and young people continue to face abuse, both at school and online. Why are we failing to stop bullying? Is there a lack of leadership, responsibility and follow-up — and what is needed for real change?
content.extendedDescription:
The reality of bullying in schools and digital worlds: the stories, responsibilities and solutions.

Despite increased knowledge and clear policy documents, children and young people continue to face abuse, exclusion and bullying in classrooms, corridors and online. Why do we still fail to stop what everyone says they want to eliminate?

This seminar brings personal stories together with professional perspectives. Drawing on their own experiences, television personality Stephan Wilson and headteacher Daria Ramzi share their stories of vulnerability, silence and courage. Together with researchers, other experts and commentators, they discuss what actually happens when adults do not see, and what is needed to make change a reality.

The conversation moves from individuals to structures, from pain to solutions. It focuses not only on problems, but on responsibility, leadership and practical ways forward.

content.title: Payment systems in crisis and war
content.description: An important part of society’s preparedness is that our payment systems work, enabling people to shop even during a crisis or war. Cash is crucial to this preparedness, but several laws and regulations effectively work against its use.
content.extendedDescription: Digital payment systems can be disabled by a hostile actor or stop working during major accidents or outages. This makes our society vulnerable and can cause considerable anxiety and worsen a crisis during a serious incident or, at worst, war. The cash system is an important part of society’s overall preparedness. Experience from Ukraine in particular shows that several parallel payment systems are needed. Civilförsvarsförbundet works on civil preparedness and has extensive knowledge of the preparations and systems that should be in place for us to cope. It has identified several areas where current laws and regulations counteract preparedness measures. Come and listen to Civilförsvarsförbundet’s presentation about our preparedness and payment systems. There will also be opportunities to ask questions and discuss the subject.

content.title: Can AI beat IfA’s experts?
content.description: For people who live with personal assistance, everyday problems become more tangible. How do assistance users solve the problems they face in daily life?
content.extendedDescription:
Come and ask your question about personal assistance and see whether IfA’s experts beat AI. The Arvsfonden-funded Assistansmiljö project invites you to open conversations. We explore the limits that working environments and laws place on life, and the strain of having other people present in your life so that everyday activities can work. The project focuses on how assistance users can make their voices heard both in their private lives — with relatives, personal assistants and assistance providers — and in dealings with public authorities.
The Assistansmiljö project aims to strengthen the rights and opportunities of people entitled to assistance to choose their lives and personal assistance so that they can live like others, in line with the intentions of LSS.

content.title: Food, microbes and resilience — biotechnology’s role in Swedish food preparedness
content.description: Crisis and war are more pressing threats to our society than ever. How do we secure access to food if those threats become reality?
content.extendedDescription:
Biotechnology is an underused tool in Swedish food production that could contribute to greater flexibility and more domestic food processing. Industrial biotechnology is developing rapidly, and several companies offering new solutions are being established. Sweden has strong technical expertise and favourable conditions for becoming a leading country in the use of industrial biotechnology for food production.

There is, however, a great need to build knowledge of the subject. What is biotechnology, why are so many people discussing it now, what technical opportunities exist, and what do we need to do to make better use of them?

The conversation is organised by Lunds Tekniska Högskola, Lunds universitet, in collaboration with FORCE, Centrum för livsmedelsberedskap och konkurrenskraft and Biotech Heights.

During the panel discussion, you will be offered a taste of the alternative protein of the future: fermented Swedish oats and fungal protein, developed and produced in Sweden.

content.title: The workplace as a setting for violence prevention
content.description: Men’s violence against women is a major and costly problem that must be addressed at societal, organisational and individual levels. The workplace is one of several settings for responding to and preventing violence, where interventions can be made early in patterns of violence — with appropriate tools.
content.extendedDescription: Effective work to respond to and prevent violence starts with knowledge. Detecting and understanding exposure to violence requires training and strategies for the person affected, bystanders and, for example, managers and leaders. A common way to develop that understanding is through courses, schools and similar institutions. The workplace as an “institution” is another setting that could be used more for responsive and preventive work. A larger proportion of perpetrators can be reached here if, for example, training is offered during working hours. The workplace also involves systematic work environment management, including procedures against bullying and violence. The seminar conversation rests on three pillars: threats and violence in working life (societal level); the manager’s task of asking about violence (organisational perspective); and how intimate partner violence is perpetrated at work, including sexual harassment (individual perspective). Representatives of relevant organisations are invited. How can we move forward with violence prevention measures in the workplace?

content.title: Fishing for household use — an important cultural tradition and essential to food supply in a crisis
content.description: The proposal to ban net fishing for household use on Gotland and in the rest of Sweden will have devastating consequences for valuable fishing villages from Smögen to Kalix. Living fishing communities are an irreplaceable cultural heritage and, especially on Gotland, an indispensable part of robust food preparedness.
content.extendedDescription:
A proposal to ban all net fishing for household use throughout Sweden is on the agriculture minister’s desk. If it becomes reality, it will be a devastating blow to countless small coastal communities and harbours, not least Gotland’s unique fishing villages. Coastal residents have fished for their livelihood for thousands of years, and the historical cultural value is immense. Small-scale coastal fishing is also an invaluable resource for our food supply in a crisis. Having people who own boats and can handle nets is a preparedness issue that cannot be neglected, particularly on an island such as Gotland. Robust preparedness needs people who fish for household use, so banning them would be madness.
In Almedalen, we will display a traditional Gotlandssnipa boat, share information about and discuss small-scale fishing for household use with visitors, and describe our Leader project Rädda kustfisket. We will also organise a debate about the legislative proposal and, if possible, offer freshly smoked flounder.

content.title: Why is it so difficult to talk about death?
content.description: There are still many taboos surrounding death. When a close relative dies, those around us often fall silent, and we are afraid to talk about the loss. We do not know what to say.
content.extendedDescription:
In the film “Varför är det så svårt att prata om döden?”, people whose professional perspectives give them extensive experience of talking about death have a conversation. They discuss various reasons why it can be difficult and offer some tips on how to talk about death.
The conversation is led by SAMS chair Kjell Westerlund. The film also features:
Ullakarin Nyberg, senior consultant physician and researcher at Karolinska institutet
Andreas Holmberg, bishop of Stockholms stift
Rakel Eklund, associate professor at Uppsala Universitet
Axel Burenius, author

content.title: No one reacted in time — how workplace bullying escalated
content.description: Subtle signals, a culture of silence and late interventions — what does it take to stop bullying before it takes root?
content.extendedDescription:
Workplace bullying rarely starts with open conflict. It begins with small signals: a look, a sigh, rolling eyes, an unanswered message, exclusion from meetings or a comment in a chat. What initially seems insignificant can gradually develop into serious work environment problems affecting individuals, teams and entire organisations.

Why do employers often miss the early signs? What happens when no one acts in time? And what does the law actually require employers to do when signals emerge?

Drawing on real workplace experiences, this seminar brings together law, organisational knowledge, leadership and personal stories to explore how subtle bullying arises, escalates and can be stopped before harm is done.

The focus is on responsibility, prevention and practical action, as well as describing the problems. It is also about “profitability”: how combating abusive treatment can actually pay off and improve the whole workplace and organisation.

content.title: Bullying’s worst consequences — how do we prevent more children from losing hope?
content.description: Despite legal requirements and extensive anti-bullying work, children continue to face bullying, abuse and exclusion. When the consequences become serious, it often turns out that the signals had been there for a long time. Why do we not detect them earlier, and what is needed to prevent more children from losing hope?
content.extendedDescription:
In recent weeks, Max’s story has touched people across Sweden. In Almedalen, his mother Linda Olofsson talks about her son, the signals along the way and a reality that no family should have to experience.

Her story leads into a conversation with people who have different experiences of bullying, psychological vulnerability, schools’ responsibilities and children’s rights. Daria Ramzi shares her experiences of being subjected to bullying and racism herself, and of now leading schools where safety and early intervention are crucial. Frida and Tilda Boisen contribute perspectives on mental health and adults’ responsibility to notice and act. Stephan Wilson talks about his own experiences of being targeted and about the digital environments where abuse can follow children around the clock. Richard Mårtensson Adin offers an expert perspective on early warning signs and schools’ responsibilities.

A seminar about serious matters, but above all about courage, responsibility and what we can do to prevent more children from losing hope.

content.title: From tools to preparedness — why Sweden needs more trained craftspeople
content.description:
Craft skills are a strategic resource for society, especially in uncertain times, and skilled trades are more important than ever in creating a resilient, robust society.
At the same time, fewer and fewer young people choose to become carpenters, sheet-metal workers, bakers and blacksmiths.
content.extendedDescription:
Vocational programmes offer good prospects of quickly finding employment or starting your own business and earning an income.
How can we reverse the trend and show that skilled trades are both attractive to individuals and crucial to Sweden’s resilience?
Sveriges Hantverksråd consists of representatives from Hantverkarnas Riksorganisation, Företagarna and Svenskt Näringsliv. Together, we work to change preconceived ideas and draw the attention of politicians and the education system to the link between choosing vocational programmes and a robust Sweden.
Conversations and discussions on stage about what the interest organisations within Sveriges Hantverksråd are doing and what we as a nation need to do to meet preparedness requirements.

Expert in education and skills supply

content.title: Cashless Sweden — the impact on tourism
content.description: Using cash in Sweden is becoming increasingly difficult. Tourism is one area affected. Many visitors to Sweden want to use cash because their cards carry high fees or restrictions.
content.extendedDescription:
From an international perspective, Sweden is unusual in that many shops and service outlets do not accept cash. Cash use is also low in neighbouring countries such as Norway and Denmark, but there the law requires cash to be accepted everywhere. Here in Sweden, shops and service outlets decide for themselves, except for grocery shops and pharmacies.
For many tourists, this creates a problem. Their payment cards often have high currency conversion mark-ups or other fees. Sometimes they do not even have access to cards that work abroad.
Cashless Sweden then becomes a factor that harms tourism, the economy and our reputation as a destination. Kontantupproret and currency exchange company Forex present an international comparison of cash regulations and the effects of Sweden’s extreme position.

content.title: Sweden’s biggest defence secret — we are complacent after years of peace, and it could become our weakest link
content.description: Sweden has joined NATO, taken the first steps in rearmament, and more is under way. But behind the new security-policy façade lies an uncomfortable question: do we have the capability and endurance needed when society is truly put to the test?
content.extendedDescription:
Total defence is about more than military muscle: it also means electricity supply, food, transport, education and leadership. How prepared are we for the need to keep all of society functioning through a prolonged crisis? And what happens if, despite all the investment, we have overlooked the most basic prerequisites for coping with a severe ordeal?
At a time of changing threats and increasing demands for cooperation, it is high time to ask whether we have our most fundamental security in order — or whether we are dangerously naive about what it takes to keep Sweden running when it really matters.

content.title: What benefits can energy communities bring to local electricity grids?
content.description: The EU has chosen to highlight energy communities as a central element of its energy transition policy, but their impact in Sweden is still limited. What benefits can energy communities actually bring to local electricity grids, and what is needed to unlock them?
content.extendedDescription:
In theory, energy communities can contribute to greater flexibility, reduced pressure on the electricity grid and stronger local security of supply. By combining modern digital control and forecasting with local electricity generation, storage and flexibility, energy communities could theoretically enable more efficient use of existing grid resources.

In this session, we bring together experts to discuss the role of energy communities in Sweden’s electricity system. What is the situation today, and which technical solutions and policy developments are needed for further progress?

content.title: Cash as protection for the most vulnerable
content.description: A cashless society affects more people than we think. These include women experiencing violence who need cash to escape, and older people who need help with shopping.
content.extendedDescription:
As Sweden becomes increasingly cashless, vulnerable groups are affected. In some cases, it increases the risk of crime. Two examples are women in violent or threatening relationships and older people receiving home help or living in care homes who need others to help with everyday shopping. Handing over cards and PINs is not permitted, but often happens out of necessity. This also exposes older people to the risk of their cards being misused and causes considerable anxiety.
Few people know about these consequences of a cashless society, and the question is whether our decision-makers were aware of them when cash regulations were decided. In practice, the market will now have to ensure that these vulnerable groups can manage by accepting cash.

content.title: How is the Nordic man doing — how does he view his life and his role as a man?
content.description: How are men in Sweden and the Nordic region really doing? How do they view their quality of life, their role as men, their relationships and their emotional lives? What do they think about politics?

The study, the first of its kind, maps quality of life, social relationships, views on gender and equality, political attitudes and emotional well-being among Nordic men.
The study gives us opportunities to understand men’s situation in Sweden and the Nordic region at a time of rapid social change. How do norms, politics and developments in society affect Nordic men’s everyday lives and confidence in the future?

Equimondo, which is conducting the study for Nordiska ministerrådet, has previously conducted similar surveys in the USA and the United Kingdom.

content.title: How much do you want to know about your future health? Technology, prediction and ethics in healthcare
content.description: Healthcare is digitalising rapidly, and AI creates new opportunities to prevent disease and make early diagnoses by analysing large datasets. This offers great potential but also raises questions: how much do I want to know about my future, and how can we best use the technology today?
content.extendedDescription:
Healthcare is digitalising rapidly, and new technology creates entirely new opportunities to prevent disease, detect risks early and provide more personalised care. Developments in AI in particular make it possible to analyse large volumes of health data, including information from healthcare and data that people collect themselves about their health, habits and behaviour. Using these data, we can identify patterns, calculate disease risks and create new possibilities for preventive action.
The opportunities are substantial. At the same time, these developments raise a range of ethical questions. If technology can predict our future health, do we want to know? Do we also have a right not to know? How are people’s lives affected by information about future disease risks that may never materialise? And who bears responsibility?

The conversation begins with a short presentation by Prof Maria Hägglund, drawing on current research into patients’ and relatives’ use of digital services. This is followed by a panel discussion.

content.title: How strong is gender equality work in Swedish development aid?
content.description: Progress on women’s rights and gender equality has weakened in several places, while the focus on gender equality in development aid has declined in recent years. This raises questions about how governance, working methods and external conditions affect gender mainstreaming in practice.
content.extendedDescription:
Women’s rights are going backwards around the world, and efforts for gender equality, LGBTQI rights and sexual and reproductive health and rights face growing resistance. At the same time, the focus on gender equality has declined in recent years, including in Sweden. In 2014, Sweden became the first country in the world to declare a feminist foreign policy, and in 2022 the first to withdraw it.

EBA studies have shown that gender equality priorities in foreign policy and development aid have made a major difference, but have also been uneven and insufficient. Today, gender equality remains an explicit priority in development aid and is to be “taken into account in all relevant interventions”. Does this lower the ambition, or express the same ambitions differently? What do we see when comparing gender equality in development aid yesterday and today? Has the change affected Sweden’s image and its ability to promote gender equality?

The conversation draws on two published and one ongoing EBA study on Sida’s gender equality work and the implementation of feminist foreign policy.
speakerTitles: PhD in sociology and researcher at the Department of Government
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Compassion at work — can your company afford not to prevent mental ill-health in the workplace?
content.description: Half of all sick leave is due to mental ill-health. Having the courage to say how you feel at work is the first step towards help and support. But when should you speak up, and to whom? Why is today’s work environment management not enough?
content.extendedDescription:
Medmänskliga arbetsplatser is a training programme for creating safer workplaces with greater well-being, which in turn can increase staff’s capacity to act and their skills. It helps companies build a work culture where compassionate conversations are a natural part of everyday life, and listening, presence and empathy are living norms. Prioritising compassionate conversations is about more than individual well-being. It is a strategic choice affecting the entire organisation’s culture, performance and long-term sustainability. It strengthens relationships, increases belonging and can reduce the risk of isolation and ill-health over time.
When we act compassionately towards colleagues, employees, customers or stakeholders, we contribute not only to a pleasant workplace but also to positive effects that encourage people to share perspectives, take initiative and contribute to shared solutions.

content.title: From Ukraine to Sudan — meet the people behind the UN’s refugee work
content.description: Behind the statistics and headlines are people: both the millions of women, men and children forced to flee, and those working every day to provide protection and hope amid the world’s most difficult crises.
content.extendedDescription:
What role do the UN and the international community play in protecting civilians and preventing humanitarian crises? Come and meet UNHCR staff to discuss our work in places including the Middle East, Sudan, Afghanistan and Ukraine.
What is everyday life like for people forced to leave their homes? How do UNHCR and the UN protect displaced people, and what role does Sweden play in international efforts? What does the Refugee Convention actually mean, and how are displaced people affected when aid decreases while conflicts and crises continue to drive people from their homes?
You are warmly invited to talk with us about everything from the situation in the world’s largest refugee crises to how humanitarian work operates in practice, from emergency responses in war and disasters to long-term solutions helping people rebuild their lives — or about what gives us hope at a time when millions of people are displaced.

content.title: Critical minerals — security of supply and choices in a new geopolitical landscape
content.description: Access to critical minerals has increasingly become a matter of national security for countries inside and outside Europe, against a backdrop of growing geopolitical tensions and Chinese dominance in processing and mineral extraction.
content.extendedDescription:
New trading coalitions for critical minerals are forming rapidly in the wake of the new world order. The EU is Sweden’s foremost alliance partner, but as a mineral-producing country, we also need an ambitious strategy of our own to secure self-sufficiency.

In this conversation, we discuss a roadmap for a long-term, fair and effective Swedish mineral supply, starting from national security, preparedness and technological development. How does Swedish mineral extraction affect Sweden’s security and alliances with other countries? To what extent can technological development and the circular economy help create resilient supply chains? Can we assess which minerals are critical as innovation accelerates? And how do we create greater public acceptance of increased exports and extraction of different minerals?

The conversation is organised by LTH, Lunds universitet in collaboration with Mistra Mineral Governance. Moderator: Lollo Pierce
speakerTitles: Senior lecturer in environmental and energy systems
Head of unit at FOI and senior researcher

content.title: Resilience and Growth in a New World Order - Geopolitical and Economic Landscape
content.description: The global geopolitical and economic landscape is being reshaped, creating both challenges and opportunities. This new era of increased volatility, evolving alliances, and shifting trade flows demand new approaches to resilience, competitiveness and long-term growth. We are in a new world order.
content.extendedDescription:
The global map has been redrawn. We are now operating in a new global order defined by strategic competition between the US, Europe, China, and rising powers such as India. This realignment is transforming policy frameworks, international relations, supply chains and capital flows, creating a more complex landscape of risk and opportunity.
This panel will discuss the geopolitical forces shaping the global economy and the strategic responses required to navigate shifting alliances and changing trade patterns – while turning geopolitical risk into competitive advantage.

With high-level speakers from politics, finance, and industry, this discussion will explore how Swedish businesses and policymakers can strengthen resilience and secure long-term growth. Citi and Dagens Industri will co-host a forum in Almedalen to discuss these questions.

content.title: When war demands more — how do we strengthen society for heightened readiness and war?
content.description: A society equipped for war is better prepared for crises. How must society develop to meet the demands of heightened readiness and war? What lessons can we learn from Ukraine? How should municipal rescue services develop to meet future demands? What does research say?
content.extendedDescription:
During a war, civil defence must be able to handle prolonged disruptions to electricity, water, transport and supplies. This requires redundancy, backup solutions, stockpiles, clear leadership and cooperation between central government, municipalities, regions, business and voluntary organisations. These are the same capabilities needed in complex, prolonged crises, but with greater demands on endurance.
What has changed is the perspective. For a long time, Swedish crisis preparedness has in practice assumed that society will return to normal relatively quickly. We cannot count on that, since the average war lasts roughly three years. Today’s security situation requires us to plan for circumstances in which normality does not return for a long time and society must function despite continuing disruption. Sweden’s security is determined not only by military strength, but by whether people have heating at home, water from the tap, access to healthcare and confidence that society will hold together when tested.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: SE‑Alert — Sweden’s new warning channel for war, crises and future threats
content.description: Extensive work is under way to strengthen civilian protection. Part of this involves strengthening and expanding warning systems, and implementation of SE-Alert will begin during the summer. How will the system affect society and the public? How will existing systems complement SE-Alert?
content.extendedDescription: Civilian protection means being able to warn, protect and move people safely when needed, with as few negative consequences as possible. One aspect is the ability to receive a warning if something happens. SE-Alert will become a VMA channel that sends important public announcements directly to mobile phones using cell broadcast technology. Cell broadcast allows preparedness authorities to send important public announcements to all mobile phones in a specific area. Through SE-Alert, the public will receive information faster and more efficiently, particularly when VMA announcements affect many people. Cell broadcast reaches mobile phones throughout Sweden within a few seconds, without requiring an app download or prior registration of a phone number. Work is ongoing, and implementation of SE-Alert is planned to begin in summer 2026.

content.title: How do we reverse the trend in serious mental ill-health?
content.description: There is great concern about increasing mental ill-health. Yet we are failing to change the trend. People with serious mental illness have the greatest need for support. How can we improve early identification, develop targeted care and make systemic changes so that more people feel better?
content.extendedDescription:
Mental ill-health accounts for a substantial share of the burden of disease in Sweden. It is particularly serious when problems begin in childhood. We are among the countries with the highest proportion of young people who are not feeling well. Mental health factors also dominate among adults who need to take sick leave.
The need for better care and new treatments is particularly great for those of us with serious mental illness. There is a new national prevention strategy addressing suicide, the most drastic response to worsening mental ill-health.
What does research say about the opportunities for more preventive work? And how can actors beyond healthcare work to take the necessary measures seriously and reverse the trend? The conversation will explore these questions in depth, drawing on current research and different actors’ work on mental ill-health and suicide prevention.
speakerTitles: Senior consultant physician and professor of psychiatry
Head of Public Health and Psychiatry Section
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Working life that makes us ill — why are we failing to change it?
content.description: More and more people become ill because of work, even though we know a great deal about what creates a good working environment. Why are we failing to change working life?
content.extendedDescription:
Sick leave linked to stress and mental ill-health continues to increase, while research has long shown what characterises a good, sustainable working environment. Despite this, change in working life seems slow. The seminar starts from this paradox: when we know so much about what creates sustainable working lives, why is change so difficult?

Alongside questions about organisation, governance and working conditions, we want to open a more reflective, philosophical discussion about what work should actually be in our lives. Are we still trapped in old ideas about work, productivity and performance?

The conversation also addresses how working conditions connect with life as a whole. Many people — particularly women — are expected both to work full-time and to take considerable responsibility for family, children, ageing parents and social relationships.
speakerTitles: Associate professor and specialist physician in occupational and environmental medicine
Professor of well-being, welfare and happiness
Head of the Employer Policy Department
Head of public policy and head of the Welfare Policy and Communications division
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: What role do universities and higher education institutions play in competitiveness and democracy?
content.description: From an international perspective, what role do universities and higher education institutions play in innovation, competitiveness and democracy at a time of geopolitical uncertainty and global competition for knowledge?
content.extendedDescription:
Universities and higher education institutions are crucial to a country’s capacity for innovation, supply of skills and democratic development. At the same time, global tensions and competition for knowledge and talent are growing.

The seminar begins with an international outlook, discussing the role of higher education institutions in countries including the USA, Canada, China and India, with a focus on competitiveness, innovation and dialogue with society.
We then discuss the ongoing inquiry into academic freedom and the conflicting objectives within higher education institutions’ missions.

Finally, political representatives discuss how these considerations should be balanced from an international perspective and the role academia should play in tomorrow’s society.

content.title: Where are we heading? From vision to practice, building health and social care for older people for life
content.description: Ageing at home, supported by close-to-home care, is an ambition nationally and internationally. Yet many older people feel they fall through the cracks. We want to contribute to an age-friendly society that prevents ill-health and promotes health by collaborating on physical and social strategies.
content.extendedDescription: Healthcare is changing — but is the transition adapted to our needs as we grow older? Many older people and their relatives do not feel that care has come closer, despite the biggest transformation of healthcare since the Ädel reform in the 90s. The new Social Services Act requires social interventions to be person-centred too — we ask how. We conduct research and development together with older people to meet current needs and strengthen quality of life and well-being. At the seminar, invited guests give brief contributions on their wishes for, and contributions to, an age-friendly society. They represent a public authority, research and knowledge centres, quality registries, health and social care, and municipal leadership. A panel debate then follows between the speakers and invited representatives of welfare technology, the physical environment and knowledge dissemination. The panel debate offers ample opportunities for audience interaction. The seminar is led by moderators.

content.title: How can universities and higher education institutions strengthen their contribution to Sweden’s development?
content.description: Do universities and higher education institutions have the right conditions to contribute to regional development, innovation, the supply of skills and a strong knowledge society?
content.extendedDescription:
Universities and higher education institutions are expected to contribute to regional development, innovation, the supply of skills and a strong knowledge society. But do they have the right conditions to meet these expectations?

The seminar discusses their responsibilities in relation to governance and other conditions affecting their ability to meet requirements, with representatives of society, business and politics.

It begins with a conversation between higher education representatives about institutional responsibilities and the conflicting objectives that arise when balancing quality, accessibility and collaboration.
The work of the inquiry into higher education institutions’ legal form is then presented, along with how governance and organisational forms can develop.

We also include the perspectives of business and organisations on academia’s importance for innovation and society’s development. Finally, political representatives discuss higher education institutions’ future role and the conditions for fulfilling their mission over time.

content.title: The parliamentary election is also an EU election — what are Kristdemokraterna’s priorities at EU level?
content.description: The election result determines which parties form the government and therefore represent Sweden in the Council of the EU. Together with the European Parliament, it sets the direction for tomorrow’s EU and legislates for 450 million EU citizens. Yet EU issues often receive little attention during the election campaign.
content.extendedDescription:
How will Kristdemokraterna act in Brussels if it is part of the government after the election?

EU cooperation is a major part of building Swedish society, and EU membership has a decisive impact on our municipalities, regions, country and the world around us. Despite EU policy’s central influence on society, it often receives little attention during Swedish election campaigns, making it harder for voters to make informed decisions on election day.

This moderated conversation clarifies Kristdemokraterna’s positions and priorities on a range of major policy issues that will be decided wholly or partly at EU level during the coming electoral term. Time is set aside for audience questions.

Possible topics include the EU’s role in the world, defence cooperation, EU competitiveness and welfare, climate policy, trade policy, biodiversity protection, AI, migration policy, EU enlargement and the financing of EU cooperation.
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament, spokesperson on EU and foreign affairs

content.title: The parliamentary election is also an EU election — what are Centerpartiet’s priorities at EU level?
content.description: The election result determines which parties form the government and therefore represent Sweden in the Council of the EU. Together with the European Parliament, it sets the direction for tomorrow’s EU and legislates for 450 million EU citizens. Yet EU issues often receive little attention during the election campaign.
content.extendedDescription:
How will Centerpartiet act in Brussels if it is part of the government after the election?

EU cooperation is a major part of building Swedish society, and EU membership has a decisive impact on our municipalities, regions, country and the world around us. Despite EU policy’s central influence on society, it often receives little attention during Swedish election campaigns, making it harder for voters to make informed decisions on election day.

This moderated conversation clarifies Centerpartiet’s positions and priorities on a range of major policy issues that will be decided wholly or partly at EU level during the coming electoral term. Time is set aside for audience questions.

Possible topics include the EU’s role in the world, defence cooperation, EU competitiveness and welfare, climate policy, trade policy, biodiversity protection, AI, migration policy, EU enlargement and the financing of EU cooperation.

content.title: Work-related crime in construction — does the Swedish model work?
content.description: In recent years, work-related crime in Sweden’s construction sector has received increasing attention. Some initiatives and measures are being taken, both by the industry and by politicians. Yet the problem remains enormous.
content.extendedDescription:
The greatest problems are found among companies that employ a large proportion of foreign workers. This is still a group that too often falls through the cracks. Who is actually responsible for foreign workers who are not unionised?
This seminar discusses the most pressing issues surrounding work-related crime, with one central question: does the Swedish model work? If the answer is no, how do we make it work?

Together with several industry actors, Bostadspolitik.se organises the natural arena for housing policy in Almedalen, at Clarion Hotel Wisby (Paviljongen) on Tuesday and Wednesday.

content.title: Sweden and Russia: now and in the future
content.description: Russia’s aggressive policy, culminating in a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, made the Putin regime a threat to Sweden. At the same time, a strategic vision towards Russia is lacking. What can Sweden do to safeguard its interests? How can pro-democracy Russians contribute to this work?
content.extendedDescription:
The non-profit association Antikrigskommittén i Sverige “Russians Against War” was founded in May 2022 and is based in Stockholm, Sweden. Our movement’s main mission is to unite all citizens of the Russian Federation and all Russian speakers in Sweden who protest against the illegal war unleashed in Ukraine by Putin and his regime.

Our goals:
- Develop a democratic anti-war movement among people from Russia in Sweden. Support civil society in Russia and grassroots initiatives promoting democratic development and anti-war activism in Russia and other countries.
- Give full support to Ukraine in its struggle against Russia’s invasion.
- Combat the Russian state’s disinformation and propaganda, and counter actions that destabilise democratic institutions in Sweden.

Come and learn more about us, our work, our perspectives and current developments in Russia.

content.title: Sweden and Russia: now and in the future
content.description: Russia’s aggressive policy, culminating in a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, made the Putin regime a threat to Sweden. At the same time, a strategic vision towards Russia is lacking. What can Sweden do to safeguard its interests? How can pro-democracy Russians contribute to this work?
content.extendedDescription:
The non-profit association Antikrigskommittén i Sverige “Russians Against War” was founded in May 2022 and is based in Stockholm, Sweden. Our movement’s main mission is to unite all citizens of the Russian Federation and all Russian speakers in Sweden who protest against the illegal war unleashed in Ukraine by Putin and his regime.

Our goals:
- Develop a democratic anti-war movement among people from Russia in Sweden. Support civil society in Russia and grassroots initiatives promoting democratic development and anti-war activism in Russia and other countries.
- Give full support to Ukraine in its struggle against Russia’s invasion.
- Combat the Russian state’s disinformation and propaganda, and counter actions that destabilise democratic institutions in Sweden.

Come and learn more about us, our work, our perspectives and current developments in Russia.
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: What were the consequences of the use of nuclear weapons in Hiroshima and Nagasaki 80 years ago?
content.description: After the US atomic bombing in 1945, the consequences were catastrophic. The scars are still visible among the city’s inhabitants, almost all of whom have a connection to the lives lost or devastated that day. No buildings in the city are older than 80 years. Today, we need to be reminded of the reality created by the use of nuclear weapons.
content.extendedDescription: Welcome to a panel discussion about the human consequences of using nuclear weapons. We will hear an account from a third-generation survivor of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, who has seen the humanitarian consequences of nuclear weapons at close quarters. We will learn how the use of nuclear weapons affects the human body and about the far-reaching consequences for affected communities. The panel discussion concludes with a look ahead at how we can ensure that these weapons of mass destruction are never used again, and an opportunity to ask the panel questions.

content.title: Has international law outlived its role? Sweden’s role as a voice for peace after joining NATO
content.description: International law is important for protecting civilians in war and for resolving conflicts without violence. For the law to retain its credibility, countries must act when it is threatened. How can Sweden work to ensure a strong international legal order?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to a panel discussion about international law.

A strong and credible international legal order based on international law and the UN Charter is crucial to peace and security. International law is currently threatened by the elevation of might over the international legal order and by several conflicts taking violent and destructive courses. To prevent international law from being undermined, the world must act when it is threatened. This is a matter of security, including for us in Sweden.

We will hear about the background to international law and its importance, historically and today. How is the international legal order affected by armed conflicts in which states consistently violate international law?

Sweden, and the world, have a duty to act when there is a risk of violations of international law. How do Sweden’s actions and positions affect confidence in international law? Does it matter how Sweden acts? How can Sweden continue to be a strong voice for international law?
content.subject: Human rights

content.title: If war or crisis comes — how does energy efficiency strengthen Sweden’s energy preparedness?
content.description: Sweden’s security and crisis preparedness depend on an energy system that functions even under strain. Which public authority is responsible for the role of energy efficiency in energy preparedness, and how can energy-efficient buildings and smart system solutions reduce vulnerabilities in the energy supply?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden’s security and crisis preparedness depend on an energy system that functions even under strain. As climate-related extreme events become more common, the security situation grows more uncertain and energy infrastructure comes under greater pressure, the demands on society’s robustness and resilience increase. In this context, energy efficiency is not just a climate or cost issue, but a strategic part of Sweden’s energy preparedness.

Which public authority is responsible for the role of energy efficiency in energy preparedness — and how can energy-efficient buildings, smarter system solutions and better planning reduce vulnerabilities in the energy supply? The discussion brings together representatives of civil defence, public authorities, the property and energy sectors, and politics to explore how energy planning, civil defence planning and the development of the built environment need to work together for a more robust Sweden.

Substantial refreshments will be provided!
speakerTitles: Head of the Resource-Efficient Society Department
Defence policy spokesperson and member of the Parliamentary Committee on Defence
Head of electrical systems and automation

content.title: What do young people themselves think society can do for their mental wellbeing?
content.description: Young people’s mental wellbeing is an important public health issue. On Gotland, an estimated six in ten young people have reduced mental wellbeing. This can hinder personal development and participation in society and increase the risk of mental ill health. Yet there is no coordinated regional effort to support young people’s mental wellbeing.
content.extendedDescription:
At the seminar, young co-researchers (aged 15–22) will present the findings, conclusions and recommendations from a research-based regional development project on Gotland concerning young people’s mental wellbeing, in which they have been co-researchers for a year and a half. The project’s overall aim was to establish an evidence base and, drawing on it, recommendations from young people as a foundation for further work to develop an action plan for young people’s mental wellbeing on Gotland.
The project comprises four sub-studies: 1) an interview study involving 43 organisations from all sectors of society about what they do to promote young people’s mental wellbeing; 2) interviews with 26 young people about what they believe society needs to do for young people’s mental wellbeing; 3) interviews with 12 school nurses in lower and upper secondary schools about their work to promote adolescents’ mental wellbeing; and 4) interviews with young people who have received counselling through a meeting place focusing on existential health.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: National climate and vulnerability assessment — Sweden’s greatest climate risks identified
content.description: The national climate and vulnerability assessment (NKSA) identifies the most significant climate risks facing Sweden and provides an important basis for continued climate adaptation work.
content.extendedDescription:
At the end of 2023, the government provided Nationella expertrådet för klimatanpassning with funding to carry out a national climate and vulnerability assessment. The work has been extensive and has involved many different stakeholders from different parts of society. In total, around 125 experts from 80 organisations have contributed to the work and the assessment of a large number of climate risks within the systems of the built environment and infrastructure, ecosystems, health, business and natural resources, food production, and water. The knowledge emerging from the assessment provides an important basis for understanding the effects of climate change and what needs to be done to strengthen adaptation efforts in Sweden.

During Almedalen, Klimatanpassningsrådet will launch the national climate and vulnerability assessment — the first of a total of four reports that the council is producing this year.

The seminar will be opened by Daniel Westlén, State Secretary to Minister for Climate and the Environment Romina Pourmokhtari.

content.title: Who takes responsibility for energy-wasting buildings — banks, the market or politicians?
content.description: How do we ensure that capital is directed towards energy-efficient and sustainable properties? What happens to properties that cannot make the transition? How do we share responsibility between a dynamic market and government policy instruments?
content.extendedDescription:
Improving the energy efficiency of buildings is one of the fastest and most cost-effective ways to reduce energy use and climate impact. Yet the transition is moving too slowly: many measures that are profitable for both property owners and society are not being implemented at the pace required for Sweden and the EU to achieve their energy and climate targets.

This inertia is meeting changing rules. New EU energy directives and increased sustainability reporting requirements (EED, EPBD, CSRD) are changing conditions in the property market. Banks are starting to impose stricter requirements, and energy efficiency is becoming increasingly crucial to financing and investment decisions.

How can banks, property owners and installers work together to overcome barriers and ensure that capital is directed towards energy-efficient and sustainable properties? What happens to properties that cannot make the transition? How should responsibility be shared between property owners, banks, a dynamic market and government policy instruments?

A light lunch will be provided!
speakerTitles: Head of the Personal Banking Market, Sweden

content.title: The brain first — guiding children through the screen jungle
content.description: Mental health affects school, work and social life. Society needs preventive measures to support young people in managing stress and maintaining social wellbeing. content.extendedDescription: The event takes participants on a journey through the fascinating world of the brain through a new children’s book about the brain and screens, which playfully shows how digital content shapes children’s thoughts, feelings and everyday lives. Conversations with authors/experts blend research with stories, practical examples and moments of discovery. We explore the brain’s mysteries and see how screens can be both friends and challenges in children’s everyday lives. Participants can ask questions and share experiences as we explore how children can navigate the digital world with curiosity and balance. The discussion offers laughter, insights and practical tips for adults who want to support children’s creativity, focus and mental health in a constantly connected world. We also discuss practical strategies for everyday balance, how to create meaningful digital play, and how parents and educators can engage children in both screen-free and digitally stimulating activities, all with a focus on children’s curiosity, wellbeing and development.

content.title: Global health in a time of climate change — what role does Sweden play?
content.description: Climate change affects people’s health around the world. The most vulnerable are hit hardest by the climate change they have contributed least to causing. What role can and should Sweden play?
content.extendedDescription: Part 1 of 2 panel discussions on global health: More than half of the world’s children live with extremely high climate risk, according to a new UNICEF report. Meanwhile, financial support through development aid and climate adaptation funds is declining. Climate change affects people’s health around the world — heat, drought, floods, fires, air pollution and ecosystem changes make people ill and force them to flee. Climate change also increases the risk of armed conflicts, which are at a record high according to Uppsala’s conflict data programme UCDP. The number of displaced people has doubled over the past decade, while humanitarian aid has halved globally. How can Swedish stakeholders play a constructive role in evidence-based adaptation to an increasingly changed climate and in caring for those affected?
