content.title: When will housing truly become a gender equality issue?
content.description: The right to secure housing is a fundamental human right. Yet many women in Sweden face an insecure housing situation. Research and statistics show that women find it harder than men to establish themselves in the housing market — factors that limit both freedom of action and security.
content.extendedDescription: A more gender-equal housing market is not just a matter of gender equality, but also a prerequisite for social sustainability. In a welfare state such as Sweden, the right to housing should be a given. Yet structural homelessness and social vulnerability are increasing as barriers in the housing market exclude people from security and independence. For many women and children, a lack of available housing can mean remaining in destructive or violent relationships or being held back in their careers and personal fulfilment. Structural gender inequality in the housing market requires action from both the public and private sectors. The property sector has important tools to help bring about change, but long-term solutions require broad cooperation between business, politics and civil society. How do we create a housing market that strengthens gender equality and social sustainability? Which reforms and initiatives need to be prioritised — and how do we ensure that all stakeholders work towards the same goal?
speakerTitles: Social policy expert responsible for housing development
Head of social sustainability and business developer

content.title: Attractive and safe cities — a prerequisite for a resilient society?
content.description: As the world is shaken, Sweden’s future resilience moves to the top of the agenda. At the same time, we face a society-changing shift that turns everything upside down. Cities play a central role in this development, but what are the key characteristics of the attractive and safe city of the future?
content.extendedDescription: The green transition may have temporarily lost momentum in Sweden, but it will of course happen. This, in turn, will bring fundamental changes to our society and everyday lives. How we manufacture, consume, work, live, travel and care for one another — everything will be turned upside down. Against the backdrop of recent years’ less welcome geopolitical developments and challenging geographical developments, this paradigm shift coincides with a newfound need to equip Sweden to meet both internal and external security challenges. A resilient society, however, does not start solely in the major cities; we need to invest in rural areas in general and regional cities in particular to build a resilient Sweden for the future. We face a substantial need for investment in security-related properties, but what other investments does a focus on resilience require? How do we ensure that our cities remain attractive, safe and vibrant for everyone?

content.title: What role does design play in work towards social sustainability?
content.description: Gang crime remains a major societal problem in Sweden and, as with many other societal problems, tackling it is likely to require a broad range of measures from public authorities, businesses and civil society. Can architecture be part of the solution?
content.extendedDescription: Can the design of public spaces help break the hold that gang crime has on Sweden? At first glance, the idea may seem absurd, but there is clear evidence that relatively straightforward architectural measures can make places safer. Looking deeper into the issue, behavioural science also provides grounds for arguing that well-maintained, attractively designed residential areas that inspire pride could be an important tool for curbing gangs’ recruitment of young people. One might then wonder whether there is a universal formula. Although the answer is probably no, there should be common factors in areas that might otherwise be vulnerable but where gangs have failed to gain a foothold. Can pleasant environments contribute to social sustainability? If so, how can the built environment sector join forces to improve existing and new areas? What good examples can we learn from?

content.title: Are ugly buildings all we can build today?
content.description: The debate about the proposed Nobel Center highlights modern architecture and a social climate in which questioning has become the rule rather than the exception. Is there an architectural approach everyone can agree on, and is design a matter for the public or a select few?
content.extendedDescription: The physical design of society engages more people in Sweden today than ever before — that is hardly an exaggeration. Divided opinions about modern design are by no means a uniquely Swedish phenomenon, however; elsewhere in the Nordic region, in Europe and even globally, people are starting to use modern technology to organise around their aesthetic dissatisfaction. And yes, some buildings being built today are ugly, but has that not always been the case, and is beauty not in the eye of the beholder? Is all architecture not a product of its time? Of course, one could engage in various forms of hair-splitting and other rhetorical devices, but the debate about modern architecture also raises some interesting questions. Why is today’s architecture so polarising? Is all modern architecture really ugly, or does the revolt against it express something deeper? Can and should architects take greater account of the spirit of the times?
speakerTitles: Regional Head of Project Development, Stockholm

content.title: Do we need a right–left coalition to break the political deadlock?
content.description: Is a grand coalition capable of delivering reform the way forward to secure Sweden’s competitiveness and standing on the international stage? Can the parties that have led governments in recent decades set aside their pride and agree on both important policy issues and who should be prime minister?
content.extendedDescription: Like recent Swedish elections, the 2026 election is likely to be a nail-biter, and even if one party emerges as a clear winner, forming a government is likely to be tricky. Sweden’s political climate increasingly resembles a vicious circle, marked by a lack of capacity for reform, political vision and leadership. This in turn leads to realpolitik deals in which historically established parties have gradually been forced to compromise their fundamental values to gain or retain power. How can this vicious circle be broken? Could Sweden be in (desperate) need of a grand coalition across established bloc boundaries, in which Socialdemokraterna and Moderaterna join forces with support from one of the centrist parties? Can these governing parties forget old grievances and agree to break the deadlock in Swedish politics, then pursue a clear reform agenda aimed at strengthening Swedish competitiveness and Sweden’s reputation? What lessons can we learn at national level from municipalities that have made it work?
speakerTitles: Chair of the Municipal Executive Board
Director of Environment and Urban Development

content.title: The parliamentary election is also an EU election — what are Socialdemokraterna’s priorities at EU level?
content.description: The election result determines which parties form the government and therefore represent Sweden in the Council of the EU. Together with the European Parliament, it sets the direction for tomorrow’s EU and legislates for 450 million EU citizens. Yet EU issues often receive little attention during the election campaign.
content.extendedDescription:
How will Socialdemokraterna act in Brussels if it is part of the government after the election?

EU cooperation is a major part of building Swedish society, and EU membership has a decisive impact on our municipalities, regions, country and the world around us. Despite EU policy’s central influence on society, it often receives little attention during Swedish election campaigns, making it harder for voters to make informed decisions on election day.

This moderated conversation clarifies Socialdemokraterna’s positions and priorities on a range of major policy issues that will be decided wholly or partly at EU level during the coming electoral term. Time is set aside for audience questions.

Possible topics include the EU’s role in the world, defence cooperation, EU competitiveness and welfare, climate policy, trade policy, biodiversity protection, AI, migration policy, EU enlargement and the financing of EU cooperation.

content.title: Unequal participation — what happens to democracy when voices are excluded?
content.description: Voluntary engagement is a cornerstone of democracy. But what happens when routes into voluntary associations are unequal and smaller voices are silenced or diminished?
content.extendedDescription:
Voluntary engagement builds Sweden every day and is a vital force in democracy. But routes into voluntary associations are not equal. Recurring surveys show that it is primarily people with higher education, established networks and previous experience of voluntary associations who find their way in and gain influence, while others face higher barriers despite a strong desire to get involved.

We also see a paradox: demands for professionalisation, administration and structure in civil society are increasing, while most organisations and associations still rely largely on voluntary engagement, often with only a few employees. What then happens to smaller initiatives, local efforts and the voices that already have the least space? And what does it mean for democracy when people start hesitating to engage with issues that matter to them for fear of stigma, being treated with suspicion, hatred or threats?
speakerTitles: Member of Parliament, Chair of the Parliamentary Committee on Cultural Affairs

content.title: Is Sweden ready for the EU’s new competitiveness policy — how do we work towards a smarter EU budget?

content.title: A strong democracy — reality or utopia for today’s young people?
content.description: Sweden and the other Nordic countries are characterised by open, trust-based democracies and strong institutions. But how can we safeguard democracy in the future in a world where today’s young people are inundated with disinformation, not least online? Is an age limit for social media the solution?
content.extendedDescription:
AI and global tech giants have led to today’s young people growing up in a digital environment characterised by disinformation, polarisation and algorithm-driven interactions. This development brings entirely new challenges, including for our Nordic democracies.
How are young people affected, and how does it affect their view of democracy? Above all, where can today’s young people find faith in a strong democracy in the future? What role do schools play, for example? Should we follow the same path as Denmark, for instance, and introduce an age limit for social media?
At the event, we will discuss how to strengthen democratic resilience among young people, drawing in part on a brand-new Nordic analysis of digital media’s impact on children and young people.
The Nordplus Junior Aurora Award 2026 will also be presented at the event. The award recognises good examples of successful exchanges and cooperation in education for teachers, school leaders, children and young people in the Nordic and Baltic countries.
A light breakfast will be served to the audience.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: From crisis to strength — how can Sweden succeed in an uncertain world?
content.description: Strengthening Sweden’s total defence is primarily a matter of security — but also a strategic opportunity for business. How can companies’ capacity for innovation strengthen Sweden’s preparedness and defence as well as our long-term competitiveness? What is needed to turn a crisis into a concerted effort?
content.extendedDescription:
The global arena is in turmoil, and the security situation has changed drastically in just a few years. Armed conflicts are flaring up in our region, trade barriers are being erected, and foreign policy is characterised by uncertainty. NATO is demanding greater preparedness and stronger defence capabilities, while the EU is increasingly talking about strategic autonomy to strengthen competitiveness.

At the same time, Sweden is relatively well equipped compared with many other countries. We are a leading knowledge-based nation with stable democratic institutions. With a strong and innovative business sector, Sweden is well placed to turn uncertainty into transformation and greater competitiveness.

In times of war, trade disputes and geopolitical turmoil, it is important to see not only risks but also opportunities for innovation, exports and new partnerships. Does Sweden have the capacity to succeed? And what does that require of politicians, public authorities and companies?

content.title: Civil society’s contribution during fires, crises and war — what can we learn from Ukraine?
content.description: Civil society has an important role during fires, crises and war. Fire and rescue services are responsible for preventive fire safety, but resources vary between municipalities. Strengthening fire safety and crisis preparedness requires a national initiative that includes civil society and fire and rescue services.
content.extendedDescription:
In Ukraine, civil society makes a major contribution to supporting fire and rescue services. Sweden lacks a coordinating function that can draw on the knowledge and experience of trade associations and other organisations in preventive fire safety work. At the same time, municipal fire and rescue services are expected to take on new and expanded civil defence duties. However, these increased demands have not been accompanied by clear national initiatives. Should Myndigheten för civilt försvar be given a national coordinating remit for all stakeholders working on preventive fire safety? And what lessons can Sweden learn from Ukraine, where organisations and public bodies work together?
The seminar will be held in English.
speakerTitles: Head of Unit, Fire and Rescue Services Department

content.title: Students’ Role in Total Defence: What can we Learn From the Nordic and Baltic Countries?
content.description: Total defence involves the whole of society, including students and higher education institutions. However, it is not always clear how students can and should contribute. How can students support total defence, and what can we learn from our Nordic and Baltic neighbours?
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar explores the role of students in total defence, with a particular focus on how student unions contribute to strengthening democratic values. To provide an international perspective and opportunities for learning, we invite representatives from Nordic and Baltic student organisations to share how they work with these issues.
The discussion will address questions such as: How do students view their role in total defence? How do student unions work with these issues, and what do they contribute? Is there greater awareness among students in the Nordic and Baltic countries than in Sweden? What similarities and differences can we identify? What can we learn from one another?
The discussion will be held in English.

content.title: Renovation and placemaking with social consideration — for safer, more attractive cities?
content.description: Can renovation make residential areas more attractive and sustainable without creating new divides? Does activating public spaces help improve both individual places and whole neighbourhoods, increasing safety and long-term appeal?
content.extendedDescription:
A large proportion of Sweden’s residential areas are approaching a point where extensive renovation is required. At the same time, the perceived attractiveness of these areas is a challenge. Many households also have tight finances, making it necessary to keep rent increases down. Careful renovation and development of the housing stock take tenants’ finances into account and avoid unnecessary relocations.

Alongside this, work to activate public spaces is becoming increasingly important. Actively developing the activities, identity and use of places can improve both individual places and entire neighbourhoods — resulting in greater safety, more businesses and activities, and a more attractive everyday life.
The seminar presents these two perspectives as different but complementary parts of the work towards social sustainability. Under the heading “Steal an idea”, practical examples are presented that can inspire and be applied in other contexts, providing a starting point for continued exchange of experience and learning.

content.title: How do we make the circular economy economically viable?
content.description: In an uncertain world, circular material flows help secure the supply of raw materials. But the level of circularity is too low, and substantial economic value is lost when valuable resources are not recycled. Achieving a circular economy requires action throughout the value chain.
content.extendedDescription: Sweden needs to become more self-sufficient in areas such as critical raw materials, and action is needed throughout the value chain. The European Commission is working on new legislation, the Circular Economy Act, and has announced that it will arrive in the third quarter of 2026. The aim of the new legislation is for the EU to become a world leader in the circular economy by 2030. How can Sweden’s recycling industry play a decisive role in developing a circular economy — tomorrow as well? The seminar discusses the opportunities for the recycling industry and its partners to be key players in the circular economy, as well as the economic challenges facing the industry.

content.title: As the world changes: how do we create a resilient health system?
content.description: Extreme climate events such as heatwaves and heavy rainfall are becoming more frequent and more intense in Sweden. They can interact with geopolitical and other factors and lead to overlapping crises. What do we know about future climate-related challenges to public health? Is Sweden’s health system ready?
content.extendedDescription:
Our climate is changing rapidly. Average temperatures are rising, and several climate projections for Sweden show that heatwaves and heavy rainfall will become more common in the future. Extreme climate events can also interact with geopolitical and other factors and lead to overlapping crises. Our health system must therefore adapt to new conditions in a changing world.

The problem and the goal are clear: we must prepare our health system for more extreme climate events and take a systems perspective on how they may interact with other threats. The path to achieving this is harder to map out. There is a high degree of confidence in simulations of the future climate, but more limited knowledge about the practical implications for the health system. The question is how we can develop knowledge that enables a resilient health system in a changing world.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet’s climate days during Almedalsveckan.

content.title: Extreme climate events: who pays for the growing threat?
content.description: Extreme climate events already have serious socioeconomic consequences. Our climate is changing rapidly, so we must be able to adapt to new and more intense extreme climate events. Who should pay for adaptation costs and future climate damage?
content.extendedDescription:
Our climate is changing rapidly. Average temperatures are rising, and climate projections for Sweden show, among other things, more heatwaves and heavy rainfall in the future. We must therefore be able to adapt to new, more intense extreme climate events.

If we do not adapt quickly, climate damage to the economy and society will rise steeply. Some of this damage will also remain even after adaptation. Adaptation requires major investment and is often local. Yet many municipalities and other local stakeholders have limited resources. In addition, mechanisms we currently use to manage climate damage, such as insurance, may fail in a more extreme climate. We need a clear picture of who is responsible for adaptation costs and new solutions to manage the costs of damage that remains even after adaptation.

The seminar opens Uppsala universitet’s climate days during Almedalsveckan.

content.title: Heta stubben: does Socialdemokraterna want a national boost for outdoor recreation after the election?
content.description: Outdoor recreation is good for health and wellbeing — 94 per cent of Swedes agree. Outdoor activities and accessible nature counter inactivity, loneliness and ill health. Yet the potential of outdoor recreation to strengthen public health and preparedness is underused. Which parties are campaigning for a boost to outdoor recreation?
content.extendedDescription:
Last year’s successful Heta stubben in Almedalen is back. With the sea as a backdrop and the aroma of boiled coffee from the camping stove, Friluftsfrämjandet will talk to party leaders and other decision-makers on various occasions about their vision for outdoor recreation. How can outdoor recreation and nature activities have as natural a place in politics as they do in our hearts? How can more people be encouraged to be active in nature? How can outdoor recreation help strengthen preparedness?

Four out of five children do too little physical activity, and half of adults have dangerously poor fitness. Inactivity and mental ill health cost society five per cent of GDP. This is deeply problematic for individuals, public health and Swedes’ resilience in crises. At the same time, we know that investment in physical activity is highly cost-effective.

The maintenance of our nature reserves and national parks is severely neglected, even though we know that spending time in attractive natural surroundings benefits our physical and mental health.

content.title: Press freedom and ethics in troubled times — what conditions do journalists face today?
content.description: Press freedom worldwide is now lower than at any time in the past 25 years. At the same time, we are seeing several major armed conflicts, both in Europe and elsewhere in the world. What can journalism do to counter war and contribute to lasting peace?

Every day, human rights defenders, activists and journalists risk their lives to seek and communicate the truth about the society we live in. What is it like to report from countries with limited press freedom or from conflict-affected areas? What ethical challenges do journalists face? The conversation focuses on the panellists’ various projects in Ukraine and Eastern Europe to explore how to work for lasting peace in the shadow of war.

content.title: Tipping points — a cause for climate anxiety or a wake-up call for action?
content.description: How should we in Sweden and the Nordic region approach the polarised debate about tipping points? How should we prepare our countries for an uncertain climate future and create the conditions for a good life in the long term? Who should make the right decisions?
content.extendedDescription:
The debate about a possible AMOC collapse, in which the Gulf Stream would weaken or collapse, divides researchers. Some warn of scenarios in which an AMOC collapse would mean a considerably colder climate, affecting everything from food supplies and energy systems to civil preparedness. Others stress the considerable uncertainties surrounding the future of ocean currents.
Amid this, political decision-makers, public authorities and civil society face crucial questions:
• Does the AMOC debate create unnecessary climate anxiety, or should we plan for worst-case scenarios?
• How should we plan for the future when research points in different directions?
• How are risks and uncertainty weighed in practical decision-making?
• How can we create robust and flexible strategies that work across several possible future scenarios — including more unexpected ones?
This conversation brings together researchers and decision-makers with different views on AMOC. Among other things, they discuss the measures needed for us in the Nordic region to continue living safely.

content.title: From innovation to patient: what reforms are needed for medical innovation to reach patients?
content.description: Unequal access to innovative treatments affects Swedish patients. To create better conditions, Sweden needs to ensure sustainable funding for the implementation of new treatments. Joint political action is now needed, but what reforms are possible at national and regional level?
content.extendedDescription:
Medical breakthroughs offer hope, but in Sweden the journey to the patient is getting longer. Defending our position as a leading life science nation requires a shift in which we look beyond the short-term price tag.

New treatments should be viewed as an investment in society, with their cost weighed against a healthier population, greater productivity and reduced pressure on health and social care. Delays in access to innovation threaten not only patients’ wellbeing but also Sweden’s appeal for cutting-edge research. Securing the future requires reforms that prioritise the implementation of innovations in healthcare and sustainable funding.

Can greater central government responsibility reduce geographical disparities and accelerate access to new treatments? How do we make room for investments with long-term value, and how can we safeguard Sweden’s international competitiveness?

This event is part of Life Science-dagen, an initiative by the Medicon Village science park.

content.description: The shortage of hospital beds in Swedish healthcare causes deaths. Every day, patients are treated on wards without sufficient expertise, in corridors or in emergency departments even though they need admission. Decisive action is now needed so that patients receive the right care in time.

On other key issues of national interest, such as pensions and defence, the parliamentary parties have reached long-term agreements across political blocs. How can healthcare similarly collect information about, analyse and prevent deaths caused by shortages of resources and staff?

Our aim is to arrange a forward-looking panel discussion with politicians, heads of public authorities and professional representatives about concrete measures to remedy the shortage of hospital beds and its serious consequences.

content.title: What matters in polarised times? What does democratic disagreement contribute? What responsibility do we have?
content.description: Public debate is increasingly marked by sharp divisions, oversimplification and misunderstandings. In such times, it becomes harder to handle democratic disagreement constructively. Conflict is part of democracy, but when it turns into affective polarisation, trust in society is put at risk.
content.extendedDescription:
What might alternatives to the increasingly hostile climate of debate look like? This conversation brings together voices with different experiences and perspectives in a cross-party discussion about how democratic disagreement can be handled with intellectual honesty and mutual respect.

The focus is not on reaching agreement on policy issues, but on highlighting the value of good dialogue itself: listening actively, testing arguments and clarifying what the disagreement is actually about. The discussion demonstrates how dialogue can help reduce misunderstandings and oversimplification.

The seminar also highlights civil society’s role in creating settings where trust, social solidarity and democratic dialogue can develop. The conversation sets the tone for an Almedalsveckan characterised by factual discussion, listening and respect — without sacrificing rigour or clear differences of opinion.

content.description: The construction and property sector faces challenges involving efficiency, innovation and climate impact. content.extendedDescription: There is a need for digital transformation, product data, greater efficiency and climate action in the construction and property sector. We want to move from fragmented reporting to a coherent process that provides an overview of supplier data, materials and environmental impact. We need to invest in digitalisation and data management to strengthen traceability and risk management, for example. Smarter and more sustainable management of product data builds credibility and makes it possible to build sustainably, make informed choices and receive information at the right time.

content.title: What does it cost society when relatives are left without support?
content.description: Relatives of people with mental ill health often shoulder substantial, long-term responsibility that affects their own health, finances and life circumstances. When relatives do not receive support for themselves, the risk of stress, exhaustion, sick leave and reduced ability to work increases.
content.extendedDescription:
During the seminar, NSPH will present a new report showing the socioeconomic effects of inadequate support for relatives of people with mental ill health. Produced together with economist Ingvar Nilsson and behavioural scientist Eva Nilsson Lundmark, the report highlights how the costs of inadequate support for relatives grow over time and affect society at several levels. The findings will be discussed with invited guests.

The report draws on realistic scenarios showing what relatives’ situations can look like when support is lacking — how everyday life is affected and the consequences for health, work and social life. Taking a social investment perspective, we show what society stands to gain by giving relatives the right support, in both human and economic terms.

Breakfast rolls and coffee/tea will be served from 08.15.

Digital product passports increase traceability, and understanding forthcoming EU requirements and regulatory developments will be important. Good data quality creates value throughout the construction process. There are benefits to making product passports a natural part of the construction sector. They create a shared data structure that simplifies cooperation between manufacturers, distributors, construction companies and property owners. When the sector has access to the same language, formats and data templates, we can reduce climate impact, simplify purchasing, design and operations, and strengthen circularity. Quite simply, we can make smarter material choices.

content.title: Lowest price, weak follow-up and expensive in-house operations — what went wrong in public procurement?
content.description: Inadequate follow-up and a one-sided focus on the lowest price in public procurement have led to unfair competition and public contracts being won by operators that do not follow laws and regulations. Meanwhile, companies with collective agreements are being driven out. How do we reverse this trend?
content.extendedDescription:
When municipalities focus solely on the lowest price and fail to follow up properly, procurement does not work as intended. In practice, the result is unfair competition, poorer quality and eroded trust in both the market and the public sector. Instead of addressing the problems, increasing numbers of municipalities choose to run various services in-house to “take back control” — despite higher costs and limited effects on oversight and quality.

Which political choices have brought us here, and what is needed for public procurement to promote fair competition and higher quality while effectively countering unscrupulous and criminal operators? Drawing on examples from different industries, we show that the problem is not the market itself, but how procurements are designed, carried out and followed up.
content.subject: Business

content.title: Is it sustainable to tear out old floors and install new ones when they can be renovated?
content.description: The construction and property sector is increasingly focusing on material choices to reduce climate impact. But why are resilient floors so often replaced unnecessarily?
content.extendedDescription: The construction and property sector faces growing pressure to reduce its climate impact. New materials are being developed, climate data is in demand and requirements are tightening — yet one of the most effective measures is being overlooked: making use of what is already there. This is already done with worn wooden floors, which are sanded and varnished. Meanwhile, resilient floors such as linoleum and PVC are replaced out of habit, for aesthetic reasons or because alternatives are not known. These cover enormous areas in public settings such as schools and hospitals. Floors can often be renovated with a much lower climate impact, in less time and at lower cost. Yet renovation is not the norm. Why? Is it due to a lack of knowledge, unclear procurement requirements or uncertainty about performance and lifespan? The panel brings together system developers, research institutes, contractors and the construction and property sector to discuss how floor renovation can become an obvious choice in the circular economy.
speakerTitles: Quality, Environment and Occupational Health and Safety Manager

content.title: When needs grow faster than resources — what role can AI play in social services and municipal healthcare?
content.description: Social services and municipal healthcare face more complex cases and growing demands for legal certainty. AI can be used widely to reduce administration, improve the quality of documentation and decision support, counter welfare fraud and free up time for meeting people.
content.extendedDescription: Social services and municipal health and social care face growing pressure: more complex cases, increasing demands for legal certainty and documentation, and the challenge of securing skills and resources over the long term. At the same time, there is a need to make better use of the workforce and expertise already available. AI is often presented as part of the solution, but the discussion easily gets stuck on technical features. The real potential lies in how AI can be used widely — to reduce administration, improve the quality of decision support, detect and counter welfare fraud, and support staff in their daily work. The question is becoming increasingly central: how can technology contribute to more efficient use of resources, strengthen legal certainty and free up more time for the core task — meeting people?

content.title: Do we need a sustainable economy and ecological recycling agriculture for a climate-safe world?
content.description: There are no new markets or raw material resources beyond Earth. Must we not therefore develop an economy and agriculture that operate within the planet’s ecological limits?
content.extendedDescription:
What should our economic priorities be if we want a climate-safe world?
- Lower emissions and resource consumption?
- Resilient food production and protection of ecosystems?
- Renewable energy and more efficient energy use?
- Reuse of materials and long-lasting products?
- Creating wellbeing without destroying future living conditions?

Is an important part of this ecological recycling agriculture that aims to:
- Build soil fertility naturally and strengthen biodiversity?
- Reduce chemical inputs?
- Connect livestock farming and crop production to create a cycle that reduces nitrogen losses to the environment and improves water retention?
- Make food supply more robust and reduce vulnerability during climate crises?

Does today’s economy create climate problems because it relies heavily on:
- Constant material growth?
- Fossil energy and large greenhouse gas emissions?
- High resource consumption and linear flows?

content.title: What happens to healthcare when patients can access the world’s medical knowledge in seconds?
content.description: When patients gain immediate access to the world’s medical knowledge, it changes more than the patient’s role — it challenges the foundations of healthcare. Knowledge is no longer scarce, and patients’ expectations are shaped by faster, more precise digital services.
content.extendedDescription: When patients gain immediate access to the world’s collective medical knowledge, it changes more than the patient’s role — it challenges the very foundations of today’s healthcare. For managers and staff, this means a new strategic reality: knowledge is no longer a scarce resource, and patients’ expectations are shaped by digital services that work faster, more precisely and more accessibly than many public systems. The seminar addresses how healthcare can respond proactively to this change, focusing on leadership, governance and responsibility. The question is not whether this development is coming, but how healthcare can lead it — before it starts leading us — and which strategic choices are needed to strengthen both patient safety and quality of care.

content.title: How important is the indoor climate in Sweden’s buildings for our wellbeing?
content.description: The indoor environment plays a much greater role in public health than we often realise. How can we improve the indoor climate and strengthen our wellbeing?
content.extendedDescription:
Daylight is a fundamental requirement, not only in architecture but also for human existence and wellbeing. Light creates a logical and meaningful whole in our lives and is highly important for our health and comfort. Did you know that people in our part of the world spend 90% of their time indoors?
A new report from VELUX shows that many Swedes are negatively affected by their home environment, while opportunities to improve it differ greatly between groups. Healthy homes are therefore not just a matter of individual choices, but of equality, housing policy and public health.
Welcome to a session exploring what makes a good indoor climate and how daylight affects public health in our communities.

content.title: Digital sovereignty through standards and open-source software in libraries and public authorities
content.description: Standards implemented in open-source software enable data portability and appropriate handling of digital assets. Digital sovereignty requires organisations to have control over information that needs protection. How should libraries and public authorities handle such information?
content.extendedDescription:
To avoid lock-in and unwanted dependencies, using standards implemented in open-source software is essential for solutions to enable data portability and interoperability.

For individuals and public organisations, it is crucial to have full control over how information that needs protection is processed when different solutions are used. Standards and open-source software are becoming increasingly important for the appropriate handling and management of digital assets.

This seminar addresses research findings on the importance of standards and open-source software, and presents practical examples and experience from many years of providing the open-source library system Koha, now used by several libraries. The seminar discusses the importance of digital sovereignty and how new regulations affect individuals’ and organisations’ ability to handle information that needs protection appropriately.

content.title: From trust to evidence — how do current and forthcoming regulations change the landscape for public-sector IT?
content.description: On 22 June 2026, the Cybersecurity Act will have been in force for five months. Management responsibility and requirements for evidence are now replacing the old reliance on trust. How does the public sector navigate demands for innovation, NIS2, the CRA and the AI Act? How do we move from theory to proven practice to secure Swedish digital control?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to a conversation about the foundations of our democracy. The old trust in suppliers’ promises is no longer enough — legislation now requires verifiable evidence.
With the CRA, NIS2 and the AI Act as a new reality, Sweden’s public sector faces a paradigm shift: taking back control over every line of code, data processing operation and data transfer. How do we build an IT environment that can withstand scrutiny?
We discuss management’s personal responsibility, strategies against lock-in and how to safeguard the welfare system’s digital assets in an uncertain world. The issues are addressed from three distinct perspectives: research showing the importance of Free and Open Source Software (FOSS) for independence and demonstrable security; a public-sector perspective on the appropriate handling and management of digital assets; and a supplier perspective showing how local cloud solutions and EU-owned infrastructure safeguard Swedish digital sovereignty.
The audience is invited to join the discussion during the seminar.

content.title: Can capital, knowledge and advice be mobilised for different forms of business?
content.description: Diversity in the business world? Can capital, knowledge and advice be mobilised for businesses of different legal forms and sizes? Several reports show that cooperative associations, one-person businesses and small companies find it harder to obtain the financing they need to develop.
content.extendedDescription: At the seminar in Almedalen, Ekobanken, Coompanion, Nyföretagarcentrum Stockholm and political representatives come together to discuss diversity in the business world. The central question is whether capital, knowledge and qualified advice can be mobilised to meet the needs of businesses with different legal forms and of varying sizes. Several reports indicate that cooperative associations and smaller businesses, especially one-person businesses, often find it harder to access financing than larger operators, risking constraints on innovation and sustainable growth. At the same time, there are organisations that want to broaden the opportunities. The conversation explores how more inclusive financing solutions can be developed to give more businesses equal opportunities to grow.

content.title: Defence innovation — do higher education institutions do that?
content.description: Sweden is strengthening its total defence, both military and civil. But what does defence innovation mean in a Swedish context? Is it only a matter for the defence industry and military actors, or do civilian higher education institutions also have a central role through research, systems analysis, education and experience of crises?
content.extendedDescription:
Introduction 08:00: David Bergman, Försvarsmakten, and Birgitta Bergvall-Kåreborn, CTF steering group.

Systems critical to society are closely interconnected and technically complex. They determine Sweden’s resilience during crises and heightened readiness. How can these systems be developed to be resilient by design — robust, adaptable and capable of being scaled up and used for both civilian and military needs?
The conversation connects to the need to strengthen the scientific foundations of systemic resilience, bringing together technology, medicine/health, law and defence science to analyse how crises spread between energy, health and infrastructure systems, and how vulnerabilities can be identified before a crisis escalates. Energy systems, medical preparedness, law, security of supply and critical infrastructure are central to total defence. The question is how to create a coherent knowledge and innovation ecosystem that enables a genuine systems perspective, rather than fragmented initiatives.

Professor of Global Disaster Medicine, KI
Professor of Real Estate Law, KTH

content.title: Hourly capacity tariffs for district heating?
content.description: Capacity tariffs for electricity grids are an important public issue, but why are there no similar rules for district heating? Could we develop equivalent models for district heating with a focus on changing the heating sector and making it more efficient?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish electricity grid companies are introducing capacity tariffs in response to new regulations. The reception has been somewhat lukewarm, and we have seen striking headlines about people facing high costs. Despite this, or thanks to these headlines, awareness of capacity as a concept has increased.

Could the district heating sector build on this? Could hourly capacity charges be its future, encouraging flexibility and thereby reducing costly and environmentally burdensome peak loads?

Come and hear the findings of our analysis of what hourly capacity tariffs could mean for district heating.

content.title: Brain–machine interfacing for cognitive enhancement – when will it become a reality?
content.description: Research is exploring how signals from the brain can be read and translated into commands to control prostheses. But what happens when human thinking is enhanced with technology? What opportunities, risks and consequences could this bring for individuals and society?
content.extendedDescription:
Brain–Machine Interfaces and Brain–Computer Interfaces (BMI/BCI) are moving rapidly from experiments to practical applications. Clinical trials involving implanted interfaces are expanding, and researchers can now decode both motor intentions and aspects of inner speech in real time. Cognitive enhancement involves using technology to support or improve human mental abilities. Direct interaction between the brain and technology could eventually change how we work, learn and solve complex problems. What potential future applications could there be in total defence, emergency services and complex decision-making situations where speed is crucial?

In this discussion, we explore where research stands today, the opportunities opening up – and when cognitive enhancement could become part of everyday life.
speakerTitles: CEO and co-founder of Sweden Dynamics, which develops tactical drones for total defence
Neurosurgeon, researcher and Director of HumanLab
content.subject: Research

content.title: How can we make a sustainable organisation based on full-time work function in practice?
content.description: Full-time work is often presented as a solution to staffing challenges in public services. For more people to be able and willing to work full-time, a sustainable working environment, effective schedules and influence over working hours are needed. How can an organisation based on full-time work be designed to function in practice and remain sustainable over time?
content.extendedDescription:
Public services face a major staffing challenge, and making full-time work the norm is often highlighted as an important part of the solution. At the same time, full-time work needs to function in practice, with a sustainable working environment, effective schedules and staff participation in how work is organised.
Through Nya Heltidsresan, an initiative run jointly by SKR and Kommunal, the partners are working to make full-time work the norm in public services. But what needs to be in place for the change to work and last? The seminar takes as its starting point Heltidsresan’s new focus on sustainable organisations based on full-time work and predictable scheduling. It explores efforts to create the right conditions for a sustainable working environment in which more people are able, willing and have the stamina to work full-time.

content.title: How do we prepare healthcare for the next generation of breakthroughs against major common diseases?
content.description: Medical breakthroughs make it possible to treat the causes of diseases, rather than just their symptoms. But innovation is advancing faster than the healthcare system, and a critical gap is growing. To safeguard future public health, the public sector must act and invest now. How do we reverse the trend?
content.extendedDescription:
During the seminar, we will launch the report “The new common diseases – How Sweden can prepare for the future”, written by Göran Hägglund and others. Drawing on the report, we highlight how increasingly prevalent diseases such as obesity, Alzheimer’s and migraine now place an enormous economic burden on society as a whole – from Försäkringskassan and municipalities to employers and relatives. We discuss how short-term silo thinking and delays in introducing treatments harm both public health and the economy.

We are at a critical crossroads: failing to invest today will ultimately cost far more than investing in early treatment and modern governance. How do we break down structural barriers and turn medical breakthroughs into long-term value for society before the problems overwhelm us?
speakerTitles: Former Minister for Health and Social Affairs
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Democracy under fire: How to win just peace?
content.description: On Gotland, itself a symbol of Nordic security, we ask: can democracy survive when facts are twisted, alliances fracture, and authoritarian regimes exploit the cracks? How do we win a lasting, just peace? What happens when diplomacy is too late, trust is broken, and decisions become irreversible?
content.extendedDescription:
This panel confronts the political, moral and strategic failures that allowed Russia’s aggression to erupt into a full‑scale war and brutal assualt on democratic values. What is truly required to secure a just and lasting peace in a world where truth is weaponized, alliances falter, and authoritarian regimes exploit every fracture. Russia’s invasion has exposed deep vulnerabilities across the democratic world — yet it has also revealed extraordinary resilience, from Ukraine’s defenders to its civic leaders. Voices from politics, diplomacy, mayors and the Almedalen community examine how democracies can withstand this pressure, and turn solidarity into strategy — and strategy into a just peace.
Carpathian Sea Democracy Week — Ukraine’s counterpart to Almedalsveckan — has become a vital instrument of democratic resilience, uniting communities, institutions, and international partners. It strengthens transnational solidarity and rebuilds trust as democracies face mounting threats.
speakerTitles: Deputy Speaker of the Riksdag, Foreign Policy Spokesperson
content.detail: Cramergatan 3, location 327, Cooperation platform: Sweden and Ukraine
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: How do we create organisations where managers can lead sustainably?
content.description: Public services face major staffing challenges. At the same time, managerial roles are complex and the conditions for performing them are often inadequate. When leadership is not given the right support, both the working environment and service quality suffer.
content.extendedDescription:
Leadership and the conditions in which it operates are crucial to future staffing. The public sector faces a substantial staffing challenge. At the same time, managerial roles are often complex, pressured and unclear. When the role is unsustainable, this affects the working environment, quality and the ability to attract and retain skilled staff.
Leadership – and the conditions surrounding it – is therefore not a side issue, but a central part of work to secure the workforce.
Through research and practical examples, the seminar shows how efforts to develop both leadership and the conditions for managers can strengthen leadership as a factor supporting workplace health and contribute to more sustainable staffing. We highlight the interaction between organisational conditions and day-to-day leadership – and why both need to be developed in parallel.

Deputy Union Director, Head of Negotiations

content.title: Dynamic capacity tariffs – what benefits can they offer?
content.description: Capacity tariffs are becoming increasingly familiar to the public. However, the feedback from those already using them is not always positive. How can we achieve sustainable implementation that reflects real conditions and provides fair pricing?
content.extendedDescription:
On Gotland, we have spent 2.5 years developing a model that reflects actual conditions as closely as possible. While delivering the greatest possible benefit to the electricity grid, it must be fair to consumers and reflect costs as far as possible.

On Gotland, we have developed a model with symmetrical price signals based on actual conditions at the point where electricity is drawn from or fed into the grid. The price depends on the load at your local substation and creates local benefits that counteract bottleneck problems caused by the electricity trading price.

The project has now concluded. We present its results and the lessons we have learned, as well as what happens next. The project was carried out in cooperation with Gotlands Elnät AB, Plexigrid and Ngenic.

content.title: Do we want to, can we, do we dare – how do we invest wisely in the university hospitals of the future?
content.description: Being at the very forefront of healthcare comes at a cost. How should the university hospitals of the future tackle these challenges? Their remit is complex, the medical possibilities are endless and resources are limited.
content.extendedDescription:
▪ How can we continue to meet the demands for high quality, accessibility and efficiency from patients, education and research?
▪ Medical advances are taking new leaps alongside an accelerating digital transformation. How can we afford the investments needed?

They do not create incentives to invest in new, less expensive forms of care provided outside hospital walls, digitally or in patients’ homes. How can reimbursement systems accelerate the transition needed to meet future healthcare needs?

content.title: More time for patients when algorithms take over – but how and when?
content.description: Healthcare is undergoing a technological shift in which AI is opening up entirely new possibilities. How can a university hospital lead and steer developments so that algorithms are used in the best interests of patients and staff?
content.extendedDescription:
The major technological breakthroughs in artificial intelligence have already happened. The task now is to start making full use of the tools – in healthcare, to shorten waiting lists, use health data in research and development, and improve the digital working environment.
Region Stockholm is making major digital investments over the next few years. The region has tasked Karolinska Universitetssjukhuset with coordinating and leading these initiatives, and the hospital also sees opportunities to drive AI development. Can a hospital develop AI, and if so, what would that require? What legal and regulatory issues does healthcare need to consider, such as the rules on medical devices and procurement of AI services?

content.title: The stock market: a path to freedom or a trap for young people?
content.description: More and more young people are investing in shares and funds. Are they naive speculators – or taking responsibility for their financial future? The debate about an alleged stock market bubble among young people raises broader questions about knowledge, risk, class and the path to financial independence.
content.extendedDescription:
Interest in the stock market has grown sharply among young people in recent years, particularly through digital platforms and social media. Critics argue that a generation is being drawn into overvalued markets and risks losing out. Others see a shift in which young people are taking control of their savings, building financial security and strengthening their understanding of business and the economy.
What does research say about long-term saving? Is the stock market a casino – or an engine of prosperity? Is there a risk that young people become pawns in a game they do not fully understand? And what responsibility do politicians, schools and the financial sector bear for public financial education?
The discussion starts from this polarised debate and considers what actually strengthens young people’s financial future: warnings – or knowledge?

content.title: When soaring stocks crash – how do we protect retail investors?
content.description: More and more retail investors are investing in the stock market, but some shares soar rapidly before plunging. How can we protect individual investors without stopping them from building their financial future?
content.extendedDescription:
In recent years, we have seen shares rise rapidly and then crash – something that can cause major losses for retail investors. Many are attracted by quick profits and social media hype, but the risks are substantial. In Sweden, several small-cap companies have brought both gains and disappointments, and Finansinspektionen warns that retail investors sometimes take excessive risks.
How can we protect retail investors, improve understanding of risks and provide tools for secure saving – without scaring people away from the stock market?

content.title: Is ISK under threat – what is the future of share investing for Swedes?
content.description: The investment savings account has made investing in shares easy for millions of Swedes. At the same time, debate about its taxation, distributional effects and government tax revenues is growing. Is the model under threat – and what would changed rules mean for savers and the capital market?
content.extendedDescription:
The investment savings account, ISK, has become the dominant form of saving for Swedish investors in shares and funds. Since its introduction in 2012, millions of Swedes have been attracted by simple taxation and the opportunity to build long-term savings. At the same time, the debate about ISK has repeatedly returned to politics. Critics argue that this form of saving primarily benefits high earners and reduces government tax revenues, while advocates highlight its importance in broadening ownership and increasing household saving.

As budget needs grow and discussions about the tax system continue, questions arise about the future of ISK. Could the tax be raised? Is a cap needed? And what would changes mean for small savers, capital provision and the Swedish stock market?
speakerTitles: Member of the National Executive Board

content.title: How War Affects Ukrainan Children and How Women Unite Ukraine and Europe
content.description: War in Ukraine deeply affects children, taking away safety, homes, and normal development, forcing them to grow up amid loss and fear. At the same time, Ukrainian women play a vital role in sustaining families and society, showing strength, dignity, and resilience while rebuilding the future.
content.extendedDescription:
This event combines two artistic exhibitions that explore the human dimension of war through experiences of loss, resilience, and recovery. 1. "Silence" tells the story of stolen childhoods and the silence left by war—where children are denied the chance to grow, dream, and shape their future. 2. "Unbreakable Flower" highlights the strength of Ukrainian women, their dignity, inner resilience, and ability to preserve identity even in times of war. 

The format is a public panel discussion combined with visual material from the exhibitions. Through stories and images, participants are invited into reflection and dialogue on the consequences of war and human endurance. The aim is to create a space for understanding and discussion of the social and humanitarian impact of war. No specific preparation is required from participants, but the content includes emotionally sensitive themes.

Friday the 26th at 15.00 it will be a  concert with the Ukraine  choir.
content.detail: Silence and Unbreakable Flower Art exhibition
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Digital Europe enables human data initiatives for better health, healthcare, research and innovation
content.description: The major European digital initiatives in biomedicine provide access to millions of DNA sequences for research, healthcare and innovation – 1+MG (One Million Genome Initiative), GDI (Genomic Data Infrastructure) and GoE (Genome of Europe).
content.extendedDescription:
In 2026, an EDIC (European Digital Infrastructure Consortium) will be established to enable these initiatives. A Genome EDIC is instrumental in developing precision medicine and improving health and medical care, while enabling advanced research and greater innovation. Sweden is leading several of these projects by building the digital infrastructure.

At the seminar, we will present:
i) The GDI (European Genomic Data Infrastructure) project and its opportunities for precision health and precision medicine.
ii) The GoE (Genome of Europe) project, which collects “normal DNA” to serve as reference material in diagnostics.
iii) Genome EDIC as the legal structure for 1+MG.

This will be followed by a panel discussion with the presenters, with opportunities for everyone to ask questions, enabling an open discussion and further exploration.

content.title: Swedish schools for Ukrainian children – integration, identity and the future
content.description: Since 2022, thousands of Ukrainian children have attended Swedish schools. School is key to integration, language and security, but also to preserving identity and ties to Ukraine. How can schools meet pupils’ needs when the future is uncertain and many live between two education systems?
content.extendedDescription:
The discussion explores how Swedish schools meet the needs of Ukrainian children who came to Sweden after Russia’s invasion in 2022. School plays a crucial role in children’s sense of security, language development and integration, as well as in their ability to retain their language, identity and connection to their home country. Many pupils simultaneously live between two education systems – the Swedish and the Ukrainian – and families often do not know how long they will stay in Sweden.

The panel discusses the challenges and opportunities this creates for schools, municipalities and society. How can the education system meet children’s different needs, address language barriers and support pupils who have experienced war and displacement? What role can mother-tongue education, civil society and international cooperation play?

content.title: State hospitals in China supply matching organs for transplantation within two weeks
content.description: The rise of Falun Gong in China made Communist Party leader Jiang Zemin so jealous that he targeted Falun Gong for brutal persecution, including forced organ harvesting. This has been going on since the turn of the millennium – and continues. One question concerns transplant tourism: is it permitted for Swedes too?
content.extendedDescription:
In the documentary State Organs, multiple award-winning filmmaker Raymond Zhang tells the story of two families in China who embark on a dangerous twenty-year journey to search for missing family members. Along the way, they uncover terrifying state-sanctioned organ harvesting that takes the lives of thousands of innocent victims – even today.
The documentary is not only topical but also an important educational film about a serious, ongoing issue. Public information about this large-scale “transplant industry” remains inadequate, including in Sweden. To prevent people from travelling to China to buy a new organ and unknowingly becoming complicit in this form of murder of prisoners of conscience, most of whom are Falun Gong practitioners, a ban on buying organs whose source cannot be verified is needed. Some countries have led the way and enacted laws.
The event concludes with a question-and-answer session.

content.title: Mental ill health and psychological strain – do we talk enough about the ability to recover and get back up?
content.description: Behind every performance is a human being: a person with strengths and limits, who falls but has a unique ability to get back up. What makes performance sustainable, for individuals as well as teams and organisations?
content.extendedDescription:
Is rehabilitation only seen as cool in sport? Sustainable performance does not come from demands alone, but also from insights into handling setbacks, failures and crises, and not least injuries, as in sport. Can we learn to understand the whole person, take a step back and see what we need right now?

In this panel, we ask questions about people at work and in life more broadly. We reflect on health, strength, resilience and the importance of leadership. We discuss the organisation’s role in creating environments where people not only endure, but can also grow, perform and regain their strength when life or work puts them to the test. Strength cannot mean never falling. That is not realistic. But if and when someone falls, what do we need to do to create a plan for their return? content.title: Democratic trust in wartime – how does prolonged war affect society?
content.description: War tests society’s fundamental trust. In Ukraine, the war affects the relationship between citizens, the state and institutions. How can democratic trust be preserved during prolonged conflict, and why is it crucial to societal resilience? How do veterans view this?
content.extendedDescription:
The prolonged war in Ukraine affects not only security and the economy but also the relationship between citizens and the state. In wartime, governments must make quick decisions, introduce special measures and prioritise resources, which can affect how people perceive democratic institutions and leadership. At the same time, shared threats can strengthen social cohesion and trust.

The panel focuses on how democratic trust develops in a society living through prolonged war. The discussion highlights factors affecting trust in state institutions, the media and societal actors, and how information influence operations and propaganda can affect public debate.

The discussion also explores lessons from Ukraine’s experience in preserving democratic values and strengthening societal resilience during crises.

A new study of Ukrainian veterans’ views on democracy will be presented.

content.title: Communication in wartime – disinformation and the role of the media in a new information environment
content.description: The war in Ukraine is also unfolding in the information space. Disinformation, propaganda and digital influence operations are used to shape opinion and create uncertainty. At the same time, independent media have a crucial role in disseminating reliable information and strengthening societal resilience.
content.extendedDescription:
The war in Ukraine is taking place not only on the battlefield but also in the information space. Disinformation, propaganda and digital information influence operations are used to sway opinion, create uncertainty and undermine trust in institutions and the media. At the same time, independent journalism and responsible communication play a crucial role in disseminating reliable information and strengthening societal resilience.

The panel focuses on how information warfare works in practice and the challenges faced by journalists, communication professionals and societal actors in a fast-moving, complex information environment. The discussion also highlights how social media changes the spread of information during war and the consequences for public debate.

The discussion also considers which experiences from Ukraine could be relevant to other democracies in countering disinformation and strengthening trust in information.

content.title: Human Safari – what happens when civilians become targets?
content.description: Russia’s war against Ukraine continues to affect millions of civilians. Kherson has become a symbol of resilience under occupation, attacks and humanitarian crises. How can democratic societies support communities facing war while strengthening international solidarity and local resilience?
content.extendedDescription:
Join us for a screening of Kherson: Human Safari (72 min), a documentary by American war correspondent and filmmaker Zarina Zabrisky, followed by a discussion with policymakers, municipal leaders and civil society representatives.

The film documents Kherson’s experience from Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 through occupation, resistance, liberation, the flooding caused by the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam, and life under continued attacks. It highlights the resilience, courage and determination of ordinary people who continue to live, work and rebuild despite constant danger.

The discussion will explore civilian resilience, international solidarity, city partnerships, local democracy during wartime, the role of journalism and documentary filmmaking, and how democratic societies can support Ukraine’s recovery and future resilience.

content.title: Ukrainian culture in exile – preserving identity in times of war
content.description: The full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine is not only a war over territory, but also a struggle over language, history, culture and identity.
content.extendedDescription:
Throughout history, culture has often been a target in wars and conflicts – and that is no coincidence. Both in the past and today, Russia has systematically destroyed cultural expression by targeting artists, museums, libraries and cultural heritage in Ukraine. Questions of identity and collective memory have therefore become increasingly important.

The reality of war clearly demonstrates how closely defending a country is linked to preserving its cultural heritage. The way in which protecting Swedish culture and history in Gammalsvenskby in the Kherson region during the ongoing war intertwines with the struggle to save Ukrainian culture is both moving and highly topical. How can we jointly protect and strengthen our shared Swedish–Ukrainian culture?

The panel highlights the role of culture in times of war and crisis: how language, traditions and cultural heritage shape national identity, and why culture becomes a matter of survival when a country is attacked.

content.title: A society at war – Ukraine’s path to resilience
content.description: How does a society build resilience during a prolonged war? In Ukraine, state institutions, civil society and local communities are tested every day. The question is how societies can function despite war and what is needed to strengthen resilience, cohesion and future reconstruction.
content.extendedDescription:
The war in Ukraine has shown how a society can mobilise to handle extreme pressures. State institutions, local authorities, civil society and citizens have together helped to maintain societal functions despite attacks on infrastructure, the economy and civilian lives. Resilience is not only about military defence, but also about how societies organise themselves to keep functioning in a crisis.

The panel focuses on how societal resilience is built and sustained during prolonged war. The discussion highlights factors such as local engagement, functioning institutions, international support and cooperation between the state and civil society.

The discussion also explores what other countries can learn from Ukraine’s experience of crisis preparedness, societal organisation and long-term recovery after war.

content.title: Frontline Realities: How Does Russia Attack—and How Does Ukraine Defend?
content.description: What does the war in Ukraine look like on the ground today? How are Russian forces adapting their tactics—and how are Ukrainian defenders responding in real time?
content.extendedDescription:
You meet officers directly from the frontline in Ukraine.

This seminar provides a firsthand perspective on the realities at the frontline. Through insights from Ukrainian representatives and experts, we examine how modern warfare is evolving, including the use of drones, artillery, and asymmetric strategies.
The discussion also reflects on what these developments mean for Europe’s security, civil preparedness, and international cooperation. What lessons can Sweden and other countries draw from Ukraine’s experience?

How are Russian forces conducting attacks today?
How are Ukrainian forces adapting their defense strategies?
What role do new technologies play on the battlefield?
What lessons are relevant for Sweden and Europe?

The panel brings together frontline expertise across key domains of modern warfare: drone operations, armored warfare, mechanized combat, military psychology, and information operations. They are experts in the Swedish "Stridsfordon 90" and "Stridsvagn 122".
